Madam Speaker, pursuant to Standing Order 36, I have the pleasure to present here in the House of Commons a petition from Canadians who oppose the tax proposed by the Conservative Government, the 9 per cent GST.

Madam Speaker, I have the honour and duty, pursuant to Standing Order 36, to present to this House 103 petitions containing over 4,000 signatures from the residents of my riding of Hamilton West, including the Hamilton-Wentworth region, who call upon the government to scrap this proposed goods and services tax.
These petitions are in addition to the ones I have already presented in this House and are only a portion of the remaining petitions of mine which are in the hands of the clerk. Some of these petitions were collected as result of a town hall meeting held in my riding at which 350 people attended and not one person was in favour of this government's proposed tax. They say, "enough is enough".

Madam Speaker, I rise today pursuant to Standing Order 36 to present these petitions in the House of Commons, reflecting the ancient and undoubted right of the citizens of this country to present a grievance with the certain assurance that this honourable House will therefore provide a remedy.

Routine Proceedings
The undersigned petitioners humbly pray and call upon this Parliament to reject the proposed goods and services tax.

Madam Speaker, it is a great pleasure for me to introduce and present a petition to you signed by many of my constituents from Ituna, Hubbard, Regina, as well as members of my constituency of Regina-Qu'Appelle.
The petitioners are requesting Parliament to maintain our VIA Rail service. They point out that with the pronounced cuts by the minister, Regina will no longer receive rail passenger service. The petitioners are asking the government to maintain this essential service in order to maintain our national unity.

Madam Speaker, I rise this morning on behalf of a number of Canadians who are petitioning this Parliament and the Conservative government to do away with its 9 per cent goods and services tax and go back to the drawing board. They claim that this new tax, which will be hidden from all Canadians, will be applied to virtually everything they buy. They petition the government to cancel this outrageous tax.

Madam Speaker, I rise, as did my friend before me, the member for Regina-Qu'Appelle, with a petition on preserving VIA Rail. These petitioners from Saskatchewan are echoed in their sentiments by my constituents in British Columbia. The petitioners state that the railway passenger service as carried on by VIA Rail is an essential means of transportation for many Canadians and has been part of basic Canadian infrastructure for over 100 years.
They also mention the fact that this is an environmentally sensitive means of transportation. There are a number of signatures on the petition, which calls on Parliament to maintain VIA Rail, Canada's present national network, to upgrade VIA Rail with new equipment, and to give VIA Rail a sufficient budget to
maintain its national mandate for passenger service. That is what the government should be doing.

Madam Speaker, it is my duty to present a petition signed by some of my constituents who claim that the goods and services tax will be bad for Canadians.

These petitioners support their claim by saying that the Tory government has increased the present manufacturers' sales tax from 9 per cent to 13.5 per cent in less than five years. The Conservative government wants to impose on these Canadian consumers a goods and services tax which will be hidden. We would be the only country in the world having a two sales tax system, with each tax administered by a different level of government. The imposition of the tax will create an onerous burden on small businesses. The petitioners pray and call upon Parliament to reject the proposed goods and services tax.

Madam Speaker, I also rise under Standing Order 36, to present a petition from a number of constituents in southwestern Ontario, duly certified by the clerk of petitions, which calls upon Parliament to reject the goods and services tax.
This is among a number of petitions that I have received at fall fairs throughout my riding which, unfortunately, are locked in the clerk of petitions' office now and which I will be presenting at a later date.

Madam Speaker, I rise as I have before and no doubt will again under Standing Order 36 to present a petition signed by numerous Canadians, calling on the government to maintain VIA Rail Canada, to upgrade VIA Rail and to give VIA Rail a sufficient budget to maintain its national mandate.
This petition today is particularly appropriate, given the expressions by American rail companies of interest in operating a passenger rail service in Canada. Basically, these petitioners simply call on the government to reject the tender overtures of "Massah" to the south and rebuild a Canadian rail passenger network.

subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81-PROPOSED GOODS AND SERVICES TAX
ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81-PROPOSED GOODS AND SERVICES TAX
speechtext:
That this House advise the government to scrap the proposed goods and services tax and implement a tax system which is based on the ability to pay and which includes:
1)	a minimum corporate tax on profitable corporations;
2)	taxation of capital gains income, with the exception of farmland sold for agricultural purposes, small businesses and principal residences;
3)	the restoration of an inheritance tax on wealthy estates;
4)	effectively progressive income tax; and
5)	tax provisions which encourage environmentally sound practices.
He said: Madam Speaker, I rise today to ask the House to reject this proposal in the technical paper on the goods and services tax. We speak directly to the people of Canada, asking them to band together to organize to fight against the Conservative Party in an effort to stop the tax.
I have been across the country recently and I have seen an interesting coalition of people ranging from the trade union movement in this country, many farm organizations, chambers of commerce, John Bulloch and many ordinary Canadians and small business people who are all saying loudly and clearly that enough is enough, the tax should be stopped, and the Conservatives should withdraw their proposition from the House.
October 12, 1989



Madam Speaker, with the GST, there will be a 9 per cent tax on everything in this country: hairdressing, movies, pizzas and funerals. Canadians will have to pay a 9 per cent tax on just about anything.
Madam Speaker, it is high time we said: enough is enough. We have to stop this tax! "Mr. Prime Minister, you lied to us!"

We can do this if the people of this country stand together as one and say no. If we do not watch out in this country, we are soon going to have the taxes of Sweden and the services of Margaret Thatcher's Britain. That is what this debate is all about.
Who is going to pay? It is going to be the poor people, the ordinary workers, and middle income Canadians, particularly those with a number of children, who will pay. It will be the women who will be the hardest hit in the country. It will be the seniors, along with the women, who will be the hardest hit as well.
About four years ago in Canada there was a great debate over deindexing old age pensions. The seniors of this country got together, they rallied Canadian after Canadian, and they forced a majority government to come to its senses within a few short weeks. I can remember very well in the lobby of the House of Commons one day back in July of 1985, when a woman, Madam Denis said to the Prime Minister: "Monsieur le premier ministre, vous nous avez mentiV' "You have lied to us!" That magical moment went across this country on the television screens in French and English. Within a few short days the government across the way came to its senses and withdrew the bill to de-index old age pensions. If we could do it back in 1985 we are going to do it again in 1990 or 1989 in terms of withdrawing the goods and services tax.
Now we go across the country and talk to trade unionists, chambers of commerce, and all kinds of small business organizations. We have seen people holding rallies. My colleague for Edmonton East was at a rally in Edmonton a few days ago of 1,500 to 1,600 people with all political stripes represented and there people were
Supply
saying: "Scrap the tax. We are not going to pay a tax like this. It is unfair." In Red Deer, Alberta, just two days ago, 3,000 people in the heartland of Tory Canada came out and said "no" to the Prime Minister and "no" to the Minister of Finance.
This tax is part of the Tory agenda to change our country forever. First, we had free trade, then deregulation, then privatization, and now with this tax move we have phase two, in my opinion, of free trade. We have a tax system now that will make up for the loss in tariff revenues, and we have a tax system now that is going to reduce the burden on big corporations so they are more competitive with the corporations in the United States. It is part of the Tory agenda and the people of this country should make no mistake about it.
Since 1984 we have seen a tremendous shift in the tax burden away from big business in this country to the ordinary people. In fact, corporate taxes have dropped by about 21 per cent, while taxes on individuals have skyrocketed since the first Tory budgets back in 1984 and 1985. This move before the country today, which is rallying people of all political stripes in opposition to it, represents the single biggest tax grab in the history of Canada.
Even the Department of Finance is estimating $24 billion, and that estimate is very conservative. It is going to be more like $27 billion, $28 billion, or $29 billion by the time the bureaucrats of the Minister of Finance get finished with it. It is a big tax grab.
Secondly, it is regressive. It is going to hit the poor very hard. We have all kinds of statistics about the poor. Across the way the government is not even going to index the tax credits fully to the cost of inflation. In fact, they only get the increase in the cost of living over 3 per cent. So every year the poor in this country will fall further and further behind. The thresholds are too low. For an individual person in poverty, that individual person if he or she makes $15,000 a year will pay more under the GST than under the present system in spite of the tax credit that is in this legislation. I think that is a shameful disgrace in modem day Canada, a country that is abundant with wealth and technology and people to make it happen and make it work.

October 12, 1989
Supply
It is a tax grab. It is regressive. It is a tremendous transfer in principle of billions of dollars of taxation revenue from big business, from the big corporations in this country to the ordinary people. Because under this legislation, under the technical paper for the GST, business can write off all expenses. It is called a churning process. When they buy machinery and equipment they can write off all the expenses through what is called a tax credit or an input tax credit. They write it off at the manufacturing level, at the wholesale level, at the retail level. They keep writing it off, and writing it off until the ordinary citizen arrives to buy a refrigerator or a stove and the ordinary citizen is then going to have to pay the entire tax bill.
That is a tremendous shift away from progressive taxation in this country, a shift from the large corporations and from the wealthy in Canada to loading the tax on the ordinary citizen. That is why thousands of people are turning out at rallies, and that is why people are sending petitions to the House of Commons.
We will be the only country in the world with a two-tier tax system, with the federal state having one tax and the provinces or the member states having another tax. The provinces have said no.
I had the opportunity last week to talk with Dick Johnston, the Treasurer of Alberta, who is the treasurer most committed to stopping the tax.
We get laughs across the way from one of the ministers. I say to the minister across the way that he has not been at our committee. He has not seen the Retail Council of Canada, whose president is the president of Loblaws, come before our committee and say that a two-tier tax system and the complexities we have will add an extra $2 billion per year in administrative costs for retailers alone. That too will be passed on to the ordinary citizens of this country.
John Bulloch who is no flaming socialist or Marxist, on behalf of the Canadian Federation of Independent Business in this country, is saying that this tax must be stopped. He is saying it is a nightmare, it is complex, it is full of red tape, and it will be expensive to the small business people of this country.
I remember a hairdresser in Regina coming to our committee. Her name is Evelyn Armstrong. She said to us that if this tax comes through businesses that are very price sensitive like the hairdressing business in this
country will suffer. Many will go bankrupt. People will have fewer haircuts. They will have less expensive haircuts because of the 9 per cent tax. Much of the business will be driven underground as people open up part-time beauty salons and part-time hairdressing shops in their basements or in spare rooms.
This tax is a tax grab. It is regressive. It is a change from big business to the consumer. It is a two-tier system which will cost a lot of money. It is complicated.
We have had witness after witness come to our committee and ask questions that cannot be answered by the Department of Finance. For example, why is a birth control pill not taxable and yet a condom is taxed at 9 per cent?
If you go into a donut shop and eat six donuts with a cup of coffee and read your paper on a Saturday morning, those six donuts are taxable because a donut shop is called a restaurant and you are eating them in the shop. But if one of these big, fat, wealthy Tories across the way who picks up his donuts and eats them at home, they are not taxed because it is called a basic grocery.
Why do we have this complexity in a law that will create all kinds of red tape and bureaucracy for the ordinary citizen and for the small business person?
The tax, despite promises by the minister across the way, will not be visible. It will not be visible to the ordinary person so that he can see what he will pay. These are promises that have been made by the Conservative Party and the Conservative government time and time and time again.
Instead of having a goods and services tax on absolutely everything except basic groceries and prescription goods in this country, our party is arguing that we need alternatives to this system of a consumption tax. We are saying that there are alternatives where the rich people in this country should pay their fair share and where the big corporations in this country should pay their fair share so that we can maintain the services that the ordinary folk of Canada need in order to live a decent standard of living in a wealthy country called Canada.
We can only get that if people band together and say no to the tax, stop this tax, and look seriously at some of the alternatives. I can say to you that it concerns me when I see people like Link Nifield and others in Alberta and different parts of this country organizing a campaign not only to stop the tax but to cut back on spending and services by the Government of Canada.
October 12, 1989

Sure, there is a lot of waste in the Government of Canada. There is a lot of stupid spending like $800,000 on a government ad to promote a tax that has not even passed. I know that there is a lot of crazy spending going on. We must not get carried away by cutting back on the federal budget by billions and billions of dollars. When ordinary people who depend on their pensions for their livelihood will be the ones who will be affected.
We cannot give credence to the movement that it has already started to end universality on social programs through a clawback of family allowances and a clawback of old age pensions. We cannot give credence to the movement in which there is now a cut-back in Established Programs Financing of 1 per cent for medical care and post-secondary education. That is not the way to go when we have a campaign to stop this tax.
What we must do is stop the tax. We must rally the people of Canada and say no to the GST. We must say no to this tax that will hurt the ordinary people, the women, the children and the seniors of Canada and at the same time use our resources to make sure we have better social programs and jobs for every single Canadian and opportunities in the future for the people of Canada.
We should consider a series of alternatives by which we can get some money to create more wealth in this country, and we suggested that in our motion today.
One of our recommendations is a minimum corporate tax, something so radical that even Ronald Reagan introduced it into the United States a few years ago. A minimum corporate tax would raise at least $1 billion per year in this country which could be spent on creating jobs, on research and development, and on better pensions for the seniors of Canada.
We should also have a capital gains tax to raise a lot more money than we are raising, with the exemption of course for the family farm, the small business and the individual residence that a person has. But outside that, why should capital gains not be taxed in the same way as another dollar or another buck is taxed in Canada? If we did that we would have hundreds of millions of dollars per year more to spend on programs to reduce the discriminatory sales taxes that we already have, which

penalize ordinary people from one part of Canada to the other.
Another way of reforming our tax system is to reduce the tax expenditures now which go out to the wealthy and the big corporations in Canada. We have had study after study and economist after economist who have said that there is negligible benefit, if any benefit at all, from many of these tax expenditures that we are now seeing.
Fourth, we must once again increase the marginal tax rates on the rich in Canada. It does not make any sense that under the last phase of tax reform that the tax rate for the wealthiest Canadians was reduced from 34 per cent to 29 per cent. Someone making $100,000 will be paying a maximum tax to the federal government of 29 per cent, but someone making $1 million is still going to be paying 29 per cent to the federal government.
That is not a tax system based on the ability to pay. That is not a tax system that is progressive. That is a tax system that is regressive. The ordinary citizen who is struggling out there at a minimum wage or a single parent family with a couple of kids should know that under the Conservative party they are going to be paying more and more and more for movies, pizza, McDonald burgers which they are picking up at McDonald's, while rich Canadians are going to be paying less and less because the Conservative party has lowered their taxes through lowering the marginal tax rate.
I suggest we go back to what we had in this country before, more tax rates and much higher marginal tax rates for the wealthy. Instead of 29 per cent let us go back to at least 34 per cent, and my personal preference would be much higher than that for the extremely wealthy in this country.
Why do we not look at a wealth tax? In Canada today the top 20 per cent of our people own 69 per cent of the wealth and the bottom 40 per cent of Canada has only 2 per cent of the wealth. We are one of only a couple of countries in the OECD that does not have a wealth tax at all. It is the ordinary worker and the farmer who is doing the work and creating the wealth in this country, and it is the rich who are getting richer and it is the rich who are not paying.

Supply
In Canada the Bronfman family alone controls or owns some 459 corporations in our country; the Irving family, 138 corporations; and the Weston family, 117 corporations. Poor old Peter Pocklington is one of the poorest big guys in Canada and yet when he gets into trouble every government, particularly Don Getty and Lougheed, will bail him out. He is a big welfare case. Yet, we do not have a wealth tax. We do not have a wealth tax, but we spend all kinds of money from the federal government year after year subsidizing the Pocklingtons and the Westons and the Irvings and corporation after corporation. They make their millions and there is no wealth tax.
What will be the consequences of this tax deal? Madam Speaker, if you had come to our committee about two weeks ago you would have noticed that the Conference Board said to us that in the first three or four years under the GST corporate profits in Canada will be increasing by $10 billion and disposable income going down by $17 billion.
Yet, the Minister of Fiance and his bureaucrats in their ivory towers in Ottawa say: "Well, there is only going to be an increase in inflation of 2-1/4 per cent, and it will only be 2-1/2 per cent because the workers in this country will restrain themselves. They will not ask for any increase". Where are they living? The workers of this country are going to have to have a major wage increase to keep up with the increased in the cost of living.
You can look at the Conference Board, Wood Gundy, Informetrica and economist after economist to see that the increase in the cost of in inflation is not going to be 2 per cent. The increase in inflation will be more like 4 per cent or 5 per cent because of the GST. Add that to the regular projection of about 5 per cent or 6 per cent and the increase in inflation will be 10 per cent or 11 per cent in 1991.
How does the Minister of Finance expect the worker to take the brunt of this tremendous government induced inflationary push in 1991? Then, the minister and his naive officials say that the existing manufacturers' sales tax, which will be $18 billion by 1991, will be passed on in its entirety to the people of Canada. Imagine that. The naivety of the Minister of Finance and his officials to say that every single dollar of the $18 billion existing
federal sales tax and manufactured sales tax would be passed on.
Have you ever seen a case, Madam Speaker, where there has been a major tax decrease and the money ends up in the pockets of the consumer? If you have, please get up and tell me about it because I have not seen that. The ordinary people of this country have not seen that. When the price of crude oil drops or is dropped by the OPEC countries, we do not see the entire drop at the gas pump in Kamsack, Saskatchewan or Chicoutimi, Quebec.

No, Madam Speaker, the GST is not a progressive tax for Canadians, definitely not. The GST is a very regressive tax. The GST is a tax that will collect a lot of money from Canadians across Canada, about 24, 26, 27 or 28 billion dollars worth. It is now time for Canadians to say "No"in this Chamber, to this Prime Minister, this Minister of Finance and this Government.

If we get together as Canadians, if we listen to the people of Canada, we can say to the government that enough is enough, scrap the tax, bring in a new system that is progressive, where the rich will pay, where the corporations will pay, where the friends of the Tories will pay. Madam Speaker, they are not listening to the ordinary people of Canada. If they cease to listen, then in the next election campaign they will never again sit on the government side of the House.

I was struck by some of the alternatives that he suggested in his point program. I wonder if he could just amplify his view on the gap between the corporate tax rate in Canada and the United States and what effect that has on where business is going to be, particularly with respect to the goods and services tax and the ambience that has created. Also, will he give us his views but particularly recommendations that he may have on taxing big business?

subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81-PROPOSED GOODS AND SERVICES TAX
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I think if he looks back at the changes in tax in this country, my friend, who is a fairly new member of the House of Commons, will realize that it was a previous Liberal government that started this change of reducing the tax load on corporations in Canada, reducing the tax load on wealthy people in this country.
I remember finance ministers like Mr. Benson and Mr. MacEachen, and a certain gentleman named Jean Chretien whom I am sure you have forgotten, and another fellow who is now Leader of the Opposition. I can remember all these people bringing in tax measures that gradually let the tax load of the corporations go down, down, down. That is one reason why the Liberal Party in this country almost disappeared in 1984. They became known as the party of the rich, the party of the wealthy, and the party of big business in Canada.
I know that even my friends like the Liberal Whip were so embarrassed in those days that he was even more red in the face than he is today, seeing how right wing his party has become. I know he has done a little bit to try to remedy that, but I remind him that a Liberal in opposition is much more progressive than a Liberal in government. They are like a leopard, they tend to change their spots.
What we need in this country is a truly progressive tax system based on the ability to pay. What we need in this country is to make sure that the rich pay their fair share and that the corporations pay their fair share.
What we need, instead of a massive consumer tax on ordinary Canadians, is a progressive tax. I have mentioned a wealth tax as a possibility. Another possibility is a merger tax when you have corporate mergers in Canada. Another possibility is increasing the corporate tax rate in Canada. Another thing that I have mentioned, which Reagan did in the United States, which is surely not a radical proposition, is the minimum corporate tax on profitable corporations. Another possibility is ending some of the write-offs for excess interest that corporations can claim and some of the dividend tax credits that wealthy people in this country can claim. There are many, many things we can look at in terms of reforming the tax system.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I was interested in listening to the member. It is always interesting how the NDP can take a reasonable proposition such as tax reform and turn it into a rant and rave and turn every Canadian against the very possibility of having any reform.
Since the hon. member has turned into a political historian, perhaps the whole House should engage in a little bit of a history lesson. Each, in turn, marked the bankruptcy of a provincial government. speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to speak this morning on the subject of tax reform, in connection with the motion moved by the New Democratic Party.

If there is a good and useful consequence of the proposal to introduce a goods and services tax in Canada, I believe that it may be that it will raise in Canada the realization that the time is now overdue for real tax reform on a broad and general basis in this country.
It is more than 25 years now since the appointment of the last Royal Commission on Taxation, headed by Kenneth Carter. It is many years since the results of that Carter Commission report were enacted into the 1971 tax reforms, and things have changed monumentally since those days. The needs of governments, the involvement of governments at all levels in our economy and in our affairs as a people have changed. The complexity of the modem world has increased significantly. The complexity of our underlying tax system has increased apace.
As somebody who has spent a lot of time before coming into this place working with the tax laws, I have been concerned about that for a while. I drew out this morning my most recent edition of the Income Tkx Act. I can still lift it. It is about 1,500 pages long. You cannot travel with it on an aircraft in Canada because it will not fit under the seat in front of you. If we have ever reached the point when it was time for us to stand back and take a look at the tax system that exists to see where we are going as a nation, now is the time.

fit under the seat in front of you. If we have ever reached the point when it was time for us to stand back and take a look at the tax system that exists to see where we are going as a nation, now is the time.
What we need to do in Canada is to recognize that after all of the rhetoric, after all of the changes, after all of the shifts from income tax to consumption tax, from corporate tax to personal tax, to goods and services taxes, from manufacturing taxes, after all that there is one taxpayer in Canada. It is the same taxpayer who pays his municipal taxes, who pays his municipal water rates. That is the one who pays provincial taxes and that is the one who pays federal taxes.
Unless we can get together as a country and look at the compounding problems of federal, provincial, municipal taxes, we will never sort ourselves out of this mess. The power to tax is the power to destroy. I believe that the latest measures brought forward by the government opposite have a great deal of potential for destruction of our economic well-being.
Last week in Vancouver the mayor came to speak to the finance committee studying the GST. He brought this point forward. There is one taxpayer. The municipal taxpayer in Vancouver is the same individual who is being called upon to pay the goods and services tax.
In Alberta, the treasurer spoke to us at length about the need for provincial tax points that were being eroded by the goods and services tax. The need for reform, surely, is obvious to all of us, not just in terms of the complexity that arises out of the volume that we need to go through in order to understand the current income tax system, but in terms of the normal objectives of a tax system: equity, fairness, economic efficiency, and, in Canada, some special concerns.
There are the stresses on nationhood, the stresses that arise from the need for the regions to be able to realize their objectives within the context of this country. Stresses are felt in the west, stresses are felt in Atlantic Canada, and especially in the north. We look at what is happening with what the government opposite calls tax reform and we see that those stresses are going to become more acute in the years to follow.
Supply
Then we have the environmental imperative. There is a need in whatever measure we undertake in this country to understand the direct and indirect consequences for environmental well-being that is the overriding preoccupation of all of our people.
What we have had over the last five years is not tax reform, even though the proposals have been packaged in a document that said all over the outside of it "Tkx Reform" la reforme fiscale. What we have had is ongoing ad hockeiy. We have had a willingness to look for each and every way possible to increase government revenues, to grab money out of the pockets of the Canadian taxpayers.
That is not tax reform, that is a tax grab. What has happened to overall government revenues over the last four or five years? They have increased by more than $40 billion and yet the deficit remains at the level of $30 billion. This is in spite of the fact that for the last seven years, beginning in 1982, the western world has had an unprecedented period of economic growth and prosperity that the government should have been benefiting from. Instead, it has doubled the national debt. Instead, it has reached into the Canadian taxpayers' pockets and tom out more than $40 billion more than it ever took before. Instead, it has shifted the burden of government service downstream more and more onto the provinces and the municipalities of this country. It has allowed the Canadian infrastructures that are so important to our existence as a nation to erode and deteriorate.
The latest example is VIA Rail.
Meanwhile, the Trans-Canada Highway is in a state of disrepair and the rivers are polluted, and it is called it tax reform. What about the consultative process? We had a consultation is what they will say. We had the Standing Committee on Finance study tax reform, Phase I and now it is studying Phase II under the amiable chairmanship of the member for Mississauga South, that great promoter of grade five education.
What did they study under Phase I? They studied a package called reforms which consisted of lowering the rates, broadening the base, removing some exemptions and simplifying the structure by reducing the number of tax brackets. Simplification? Well, we talked about that before the election but really it is not as important as overall reform, they said.

October 12, 1989
Supply
The act is much wider, much broader and much heavier than it was before 1984 as we come out of the first phase of Tory tax reform. It is much more complicated. In fact the last enactment that simplified income tax at all was brought in by Finance Minister Lalonde when he simplified the rules for small business taxation. There is no overall consultative process, no study of alternative policies. There is no look at where we are going as a country or at the overlap between federal and provincial tax burdens. No, we reduced the number of brackets from ten to three.
I guess that simplified it for some opposite. Frankly, most Canadians never found it all that difficult to go to the back of their guide and work out their rate. Have they made it more fair? What we have discovered in looking at the effects of net tax increases over the years since 1984, according to the Canadian Council on Social Development, is that there has been a significant shift in the burden of taxation in this country and that burden is now being borne by families. Since 1984 the Canadian family with a poverty line income has experienced an increase in taxes of 61 per cent. That is where the burden is being borne. For the average income family, it is 29 per cent and for the upper income family, 7 per cent.
When you look at what has happened to the Canadian tax system overall since 1984, you discover that in spite of all the pro-family rhetoric we sometimes hear across the way, the real way in which it could be helping families in Canada is ignored by the Conservative government. It does not care about families.
Then there is the essential dishonesty of its approach to tax reform. What kind of system is it, what kind of government is it that comes forward before an election and says that it is lowering taxes, that you will get bigger refunds on July 1, 1988, just in time for the November election? A few months later, after the election is safely out of the way, it increased taxes.
They talk about two phases of tax reform. Phase I will lower taxes and Phase II, which is revenue neutral, will fix up the manufacturers' sales tax, that old chestnut that needs to be repaired. What happens? After the election is over and after they are safely in office, we find that the reform of the manufacturers' sales tax is a poorly disguised tax grab.
Then we have the elimination of universality, those social programs that were a sacred trust. The government said it would never touch them. People who bought and paid for old age securities in the years before 1971 were assured by the House of Commons in debate when tax reform went through in 1971 that they would continue to be entitled to universal old age security. It is gone with a stroke of the pen. Who cares about them? They are old anyway.
I want to talk a little about the goods and services tax. This tax is the single most significant change to the Canadian tax system since the introduction of the income tax in 1917. This is not a temporary measure. This is a measure that will bring with it an incredible federal bureaucracy, thousands and thousands of tax police across Canada hired to enforce it, a paper burden on small business. In short, it is a burden that will be borne by all Canadians for the rest of their lives. There will be no way out of this tax once it is implemented.
What is it? What does it represent? We know first of all that it is a tax grab. We know that the minister's promises before the election of revenue neutrality were nothing more than words. They were nothing more than pre-election rhetoric. They were simply false. According to the Department of Finance, we may raise $24 billion and some out of this tax, $24 billion compared to the $18 billion that is being raised by the manufacturers' sales tax after this government increased it by 50 per cent from 9 per cent to 13.5 per cent in its five years in office.
The $24 billion is a low estimate. Some of the estimates are as high as $30 billion. If the experience of New Zealand which the government likes to recommend to us is any indication, $30 billion might be a low estimate.
This new tax is a shift in the tax burden. It is a shift from big business to small business, it is a shift from central Canada to the regions, it is a shift from corporations to consumers, it is a shift from manufacturers to services. The government will deny this. It says:"the manufacturers' sales tax, you do not think that just because we collect it from the corporations that they end up paying it, do you? No, no, corporations pass that on, after all its the people who buy their products who pay the tax". That is nice in economic theory, but it makes one wonder why the Conference Board of Canada went through its projections on what would happen when the implementation of the GST was completed to corporate income.
October 12, 1989

The gross domestic product in Canada is actually declining in the first year, 1991, and very marginally increasing in subsequent years according to the Conference Board of Canada. Corporate profits increase in 1991 by $.6 billion, in 1992 by $4.9 billion, and in 1993 by $3.9 billion. I ask you, how does that happen? That is by how much the corporate profits are going to increase after the implementation of this tax.
There is only one of two explanations. Since we have seen from the same projections that the economy is not particularly growing, certainly not growing at that rate, where is the additional corporate profit coming from? What it means is that the manufacturers' sales tax was either not being passed on but was being eaten by the manufacturers to some extent, in other words being borne by the shareholders-and we might wonder what the nationality of those shareholders is-or the other explanation is that the corporations will simply not pass on the 13.5 per cent savings when they realize them at the elimination of the MST. That would not be inconsistent with what happened in 1978 when the Minister of Finance, Jean Chretien, reduced the manufacturer's sales tax from 12 to 9 per cent.
What else is the GST? It is a deluge of complexity. John Bulloch of the Canadian Federation of Independent Business told us that it is going to be a nightmare on Main Street. We will be the only country in the world with a fully integrated, consumer level, two-tiered sales tax with different exemptions, different rates and different complexities. Every mother and father store owner across Canada, every retailer, every restaurateur and every service, unless they are generating revenues of less than $30,000 a year, is going to have to figure out how to collect it, how to pay it, how to differentiate it from the retail sales tax. It is a mess.
Anyone who brings in New Zealand as an example of how the thing might work is just out of their minds. New Zealand is a unitary state with no provincial or state governments. There is no complexity there. It is a state in which internal transportation costs are of no consequence. There is no basis of comparison there.

The Retail Council of Canada called this new tax an unspeakable act of self-mutilation. These are the Tories' friends. Imagine having friends like that, Madam Speaker. Then there is the regressive nature of the tax. It is regressive. They say regressivity can be addressed with the refundable tax credit mechanism. That is the solution for all of it. All you have to do is file an income tax return and you will get four quarterly payments a year, making the tax progressive. We will find all those poor people, the illiterate people, the people who are out of sight and who are not on anybody's computer, and we will say: "Here is your T-l, please complete it and file it, and the government will send you a cheque." Thank you for progressivity, Mr. Wilson.
What about food? We have heard before the committee again and again, and we have heard statements by the chairman and the vice chairman of the finance committee, that it would be a good idea to broaden the base by taxing basic groceries. That would make things so much simpler, they say, and then we can lower the rate.
The food retailers told us that they were not worried about the complexity of having basic groceries exempt, that they are used to doing that under the retail sales tax systems in nine provinces, that it is no big problem. But the effect of taxing food on regressivity is very significant because it is clear that low-income people spend a much higher proportion of their incomes on food, on basic groceries, than do other Canadians, especially upper and middle-income Canadians.
Although the government seems incapable of finding a solution to the fact that there is no luxury tax, it is saying there are anomalies here, for instance, caviar will be exempt, and cartons of milk from McDonald's will not be. Surely those can be addressed with a little bit of ingenuity. There must be a good rationale for this magnificent tax, there must be one somewhere.
The government says the exporters need it. Well, those raving socialists at the Fraser Institute told us last week that the exporters do not need it. They are already getting government support and subsidies of 1 per cent, which is equal to the component of the manufacturers' sales tax contained in their exports. So it is a complete opposite.

The government says that the manufacturers need it for domestic consumption. Surely the best minds in Canada can find some way to solve any problems that are arising from domestic consumption with respect to the manufacturers' sales tax. The real problem that our manufacturers and exporters face is the consequences of the government's monetary policy, the high interest rates, 4 per cent above the U.S. rate.
What I am suggesting today is that what we need in Canada is a full review of the tax system. I agree with the essence of the New Democratic Party motion that the goods and services tax should not be proceeded with, but I do not agree with its suggestion that we can patch up the tax system with a series of minor amendments. Therefore, I would like to move, seconded by the hon. member for Ottawa-Vanier, the following amendment to the motion which is before you today, Madam Speaker, that will propose an over-all review of our tax systems in Canada.

The Hon. Member for Ottawa South was kind enough to send a copy of his amendment to the Chair prior to taking the floor in debate, so I have had a chance to examine the procedural acceptability of the motion.

I first want to thank the Hon. Member for his co-operation, which I greatly appreciate.

However, I have doubts about the acceptability of this amendment. I will refer the hon. member and everyone in the House to citation 482 of Beauchesne's which reads as follows:
On an allotted day, during consideration of the business of Supply, an amendment must not provide the basis for an entirely different debate than that proposed in the original motion.
In my opinion, the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Ottawa South does this. It takes away what is on the table today and brings a new suggestion.
I could also refer the hon. member to a ruling by Speaker Lamoureux in his Decisions page 322. We are faced with a situation similar to this. Speaker Lamoureux said:
The proposed amendment does more than qualify or amend the main motion; it seeks to provide a basis for an entirely different debate. Furthermore, when the opposition parties agree on the choice of subject for an allotted dqy, "the spirit of fair play would require that the day not be taken away by means of an amendment". The Standing Order requiring notice would be pointless if, after notice had been given, the motion were amended to make possible the consideration of an entirely new facet of the question.
Thus, with respect, I must rule the amendment out of order and not permissible at this time.

First, there was the introduction of the capital gains tax to the system which was intended to and which, until the Tories began tinkering with it a few years ago, did result to some extent in a realization of taxation on wealth at the time that a person died through the deemed realization on death of assets.
The other thing that happened in 1971 when the federal government abandoned the estate tax was that it was really given over to the provinces, many of which continued to have estate or succession duties for quite a few years after 1971. There are many problems with the capital gains tax. The first thing this government did in that memorable budget that the Minister of Finance presented in May 1985, in which it also attempted to deindex old age pensions, was to introduce a $500,000 capital gains exemption. The government said it was in order to stimulate economic activity, to reward risk taking.

I am going to discuss some of the alternatives that the New Democratic Party has in its motion and I am going to pay particular attention to the Liberal solution to the tax situation in this country of having another royal commission, another study. They did that in 1971, as I remember. We saw what transpired from there and there has been some criticism of what has happened from that tax reform today in the House.
I might say to the hon. member that in all fairness- and I am sure he was not misleading the House with his figures-income has in fact increased to the Government of Canada by some $40 billion. I think that is what he said. One of the things he did not point out, and I think in all fairness he should have, was that only 20 per cent of that increase came from tax increases. The other 80 per cent came from the growth of the economy-a million and a half new taxpayers in this country, new jobs that have been created and people paying taxes-and the betterment of our corporations and of small businesses in this country which are paying their taxes as well. He failed to mention that. I think that he should, in his presentation to be fair, have pointed out that a very small portion, one-fifth of that additional income that the government has realized, has come from income tax.
October 12, 1989

Let us talk about the reforming of Canada's tax system. During the last five years, our government has taken much-needed action to modernize and to improve the fairness of Canada's tax system. It is not done yet, and it is not perfect. I am the first one to admit that. At least this government has taken very positive action. Canada needs a modem tax system in order to meet the challenge of an increasingly competitive global economy.
Today the New Democratic Party said that we should go back to the old ways, that we should leave the manufacturer's sales tax and go back to the old tax reform where we had 10 different levels of taxation. "Let us tax the rich." I remember them campaigning on that once. "Tax the rich." That was the whole theme of their campaign. We know what happened to that.

We must understand that we are dealing in a global economy. Equally important, Canadians want a tax system that is as equitable as possible. That is what we are attempting to do.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Privatization and Regulatory Affairs)
subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81-PROPOSED GOODS AND SERVICES TAX
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I always enjoy the interruptions of the hon. member for Kamloops. He is so well informed. I will not mention that nobody is here but him from the NDP any more. I promise.
The measures that we have taken to reform Canada's tax system are part of a comprehensive long-term economic strategy which was laid out before this House in November of 1984. The strategy has been designed to produce a more competitive economy, sustained economic growth and the creation of productive Canadian jobs. It would be much, much easier for our government to let the subject of tax reform drift as past governments have done. For a government that takes its responsibilities seriously that kind of cop-out was just not acceptable.
Our objective is to have the fairest and most efficient tax system that can be designed. I believe that we have made considerable progress toward achieving that goal. In reforming the personal and corporate income tax system, stage one of tax reform was lowered tax rates. We broadened the tax base to increase efficiency and restore fairness to the system.
Our reform package ensures that higher income individuals and corporations pay their fair share of taxes. It ensures that investment decisions are based on economic merit rather than tax considerations and how to beat the tax man. It ensures that individuals in similar economic circumstances are taxed more equitably. It ensures that lower income Canadians bear a proportionately smaller share of the tax burden than higher income Canadians.

October 12, 1989
Supply
Replacing the current federal sales tax with the goods and services tax is another building block in our over-all plan for sustaining economic growth and prosperity. In this regard, it is essential to recognize how important a country's tax system is in determining the competitiveness of its economy. We need a tax system which will contribute to, not detract from, Canada's natural advantages, one that will encourage competitiveness and job creation.
In terms of the existing sales tax I noticed very carefully today that not one of the opposition members mentioned the existing sales tax, not one of them. Not one of them suggested that it be removed. Not one of them suggested that we need a new sales tax system in this country. All they said was, "Scrap it". They never talked about the existing sales tax, with the exception of my hon. friend from Ottawa South who bragged about Jean Chretien who reduced the federal sales tax rate from 12 per cent to 9 per cent just before an election period back some years ago. That is probably the best thing that he did as finance minister, I might say. I do not want to get into a leadership debate today.
When we look at this existing sales tax we see a tax that has not been fair to either Canadian manufacturers or consumers. It has not been conditioned to economic competitiveness and growth. Let us be clear, this tax is not just a source of academic embarrassment to public finance theorists. This tax hurts Canadians. The present tax is hidden. It handicaps the economy. It is very complex to administer. It is a very unreliable generator of revenue. Incredibly, the current hidden federal sales tax puts Canadian manufacturers at a disadvantage to foreign manufacturers, not only on exports but on imports as well. It is narrowly based. It is inequitable. It leads to all sorts of distortions in the market-place.
Seventy-five thousand firms pay this tax, submit it to government. There are 22,000 special arrangements and administrative interpretations-22,000. So it is not fair even to those 75,000 who are submitting the tax today.
In view of the sorry state of this hidden federal sales tax, there is really no choice but to replace it. Yet the system is a major pillar of our tax structure. It contributes more than 17 per cent of the federal government's revenues annually.
Removing the tax and building a replacement is a challenge of major proportions. Nobody is questioning that. I do not think any of the witnesses who have come before the Standing Committee on Finance have minimized the job of replacing this manufacturer's sales tax. One thing that they all say is, "Get rid of it". I do not think that is part of the debate in this country. I think that is a given. Even the opposition parties in a motion presented to this House unanimously from a standing committee said we had to get rid of it.
There are many approaches to the problem, in theory at least. For example, as an alternative to bringing in new sales tax systems some have argued, and the NDP argue this, that the current tax should simply be abolished and the foregone revenues replaced by a corresponding increase in income tax rates. Supporters of this approach argue that this would allow for a fairer tax system overall. There are, however, some powerful economic reasons for avoiding such an increased reliance on income taxation.
Our current tax structure relies on three pillars: sales tax, income tax and corporate tax. The current federal sales tax next year will contribute about $17 billion in tax revenues. To put this in perspective, if we eliminated the federal sales tax that we have now, which we want to do, and put it on to income tax, Canadians would be paying a 30 per cent increase in personal income tax-a 30 per cent increase in personal income tax. An increase of this magnitude would lead to substantial disincentives to work and invest. There is no question about that.
Alternatively, relying on the corporate tax system for these revenues would require corporate tax revenues to more than double. We would have to double the taxation on all our small businesses, on all our corporations in this country to realize the same amount of money.
Therefore, the real issue is not whether Canada needs a sales tax, but to try to develop a sales tax that is fair and supports growth. Replacing the existing tax with the tax that the government is proposing through its goods and services tax will achieve three important goals. First, it will continue to contribute to the government's ongoing plan to reduce the deficit. It will be a vital element in our plan to make the changes necessary to ensure that Canada can compete effectively in the world and at home. It will improve the overall fairness of the tax
October 12, 1989

system. Lower and modest income Canadians will be better off when the GST is in place.
During the few moments I have left I want to address specifically the points in the motion before the House. The motion suggests that we should introduce a minimum corporate tax on profitable corporations. In the two decades before our government took office governments of the day permitted the corporate tax system to become riddled with special exemptions and deductions. I agree with my hon. friend for Ottawa South when he says the tax act is so thick he cannot get it under the seat of a plane. I never carry the tax thing around, to be quite honest with you. But I guess some people like the hon. member for Ottawa South takes it with him and cannot get it under his airplane seat. I understand that. But he must remember that the Income Tax Act just did not develop in the last four years. That, over the last 20 years, has allowed these special exemptions and these deductions. What it did was encourage wasteful activity and it eroded the nation's tax base.
Let us talk about a minimum corporate tax. That is what some people are suggesting we should introduce. However, this government believed that rather than patching up the tax, which that does-it allows the same exemptions and all the other stuff but you just put a minimum tax on-the best solution was to go to the root of the problem and curtail these special exemptions. The result has been a progressive reform of the corporate tax system over the past six years. This has included measures to generally reduce fast write-offs on capital expenditures, to increase the rate of capital gains taxation, to eliminate the general investment tax credit rates, to sharply reduce special investment tax credit rates, to block the use of various complicated financial schemes, to transfer losses and other tax advantages from nonprofitable corporations to profitable ones.
In addition, in the April budget the government introduced the large corporations tax which ensures that all corporations pay federal tax.
Supply
The overall impact of these measures is that we will be able to increase annual revenues from the corporate sector by over $2 billion. Furthermore, because the corporate tax base is much broader now, the year to year variations in tax revenue will be more stable in the future than they have been in the past. This will enable the government to plan its programs on the basis of more certain corporate tax revenues. In summary, the federal government has chosen to repair the fundamental weaknesses of the corporate tax system, rather than leave them in place.
The motion suggests that we should tax income from capital gains at 100 per cent, with the exemption of capital gains from farm lands sold for agricultural purposes, small businesses, and principal residences. Under the existing tax, farmers and small businesses enjoy a $500,000 capital gains exemption and the existing tax also does not apply to the sale of principal residences.
However, the government remains committed to the $100,000 lifetime capital gains exemption for all other taxpayers as an incentive to encourage risk taking and increased equity participation in the Canadian economy. We believe that over time this measure will improve the balance sheets and the financial health of Canadian companies, thus contributing to job creation and higher incomes.
A further incentive to invest is provided by the inclusion rate for capital gains which the hon. member talked about today. The inclusion rate has been increased from 50 per cent to 66 2/3 per cent and is legislated to rise to 75 per cent for 1990 and subsequent years.
I would point out that it is desirable that the burden of Canada's capital gains tax not be significantly above that of other industrial nations. Canada will not be able to attract equity investment that is needed for future growth and job creation if we place an excessive tax burden on capital gains while our neighbours do not. For these and other reasons we believe that the present tax treatment of capital gains in Canada is appropriate.
The motion suggests that we should restore an inheritance tax on wealthy estates. Past experience with estate and gift taxes has shown that these taxes, first, were inequitable and, second, they were inefficient. The hon. member wanted some reasons why it was removed. Third, these taxes were complex to administer. Realizing this, the previous Liberal government abolished estate and gift taxes in 1971. Those taxes were found to be inequitable because of the many avenues of legal tax avoidance open to taxpayers with access to sophisticated tax planning advice and the resources to pursue these opportunities. Such taxes were also inefficient because

October 12, 1989
Supply
they encouraged taxpayers to invest their wealth to an excessive extent in those investments that for administrative purposes are tax lightly. Thus they tended to encourage increased investment in farm land and life insurance policies.
A decision by the government to reintroduce estate and gift taxes would likely encourage wealthy Canadians to take up foreign residency-this is what we saw happen before and is one of the reasons why it was changed- and redirect their investment in entrepreneurial activities elsewhere. Do you remember the famous trips to the Bahamas by so many of our wealthy in this country just because of that, because of tax planning purposes? This would deprive Canada, of course, of savings and entrepreneurial talent. We agree with that decision that was taken back in 1971. We disagree with the New Democratic Party.
I guess the most important thing, something which never bothers the socialists, is that it was administratively complex because to be successful revenue raisers, they must be accompanied by complex anti-avoidance measures. Even then, the experience of other countries shows that such measures are largely ineffective. The taxpayers and their advisers appear to be always one step ahead of the tax department. I think the hon. member knows that.
On balance, such a tax as that proposed in the motion would yield small revenues, require complex legislation, be subject to widespread legal avoidance, and perhaps even illegal evasion.
The motion suggests the introduction of a more effective, progressive income tax. I said earlier that the goods and services tax is the second element in the government's comprehensive tax reform package, The first stage that took effect in 1988 involved changes to both personal and corporate income taxes. The personal income tax proposals were designed to produce a fairer, more understandable tax system. These changes also promoted greater initiative and improved competitiveness, thus contributing to economic growth and job creation. The record speaks for itself-1.5 million jobs over the last five years. The key to achieving these goals was to lower tax rates and broaden the tax base.
Lower tax rates improved incentives for Canadians to work, to invest, and to raise their standards of living. More than 85 per cent of all households had their income tax reduced as a result of tax reform. Some 850,000 lower income Canadians had their income tax eliminated. At the same time, income taxes were increased for about one million high income households. I experienced that myself.
These taxpayers included those who had claimed large, special tax preferences or credits. A progressive tax system is one in which every one pays their share, based on their ability to pay.
In 1986, the government introduced the alternative minimum tax to respond to the growing concern at the numbers of high income Canadians who were paying little or no personal income tax. Statistics show that in 1987 there were 39,550 taxpayers subject to the minimum tax yielding revenues of close to $150 million, which resulted in the reduction of a number of high income individuals who were not paying their share of tax. Now only about one-half of 1 per cent of high income individuals are paying little or no personal income tax. They cannot get away with that for much longer than two years when it catches up with them again.
Our commitment to a fairer tax system is apparent in the proposal of sales tax reform as well. A broad tax base, a low rate and targeted assistance to lower and modest income families will ensure that the proposal will be fair.
Are you telling me my time is up, Madam Speaker? I am just getting warmed up, for heaven's sake.
Let me just say on the GST, if I might just have a paragraph, that they keep telling me that it is not fair to low income people. The GST credit will be increased to $225 per adult and $100 per child. The household income level up to which maximum benefits will be paid will be increased to $24,000, so that many more Canadian families will benefit from the credit. It will be delivered four times a year in advance. More than nine million Canadians will receive the GST credit cheques. Families earning less than $30,000 will be better off once the GST is in place.
October 12, 1989

In addition to the enriched GST credit, the middle income tax rate will be reduced from 26 per cent to 25 per cent. This will provide assistance to middle income families and make the income tax system more progressive.
I realize my time is up, Madam Speaker. I just want to say that I welcome the opportunity to debate this matter today. I thank the New Democratic Party for bringing this motion forward because it gives the government an opportunity to present-and we will have other speakers later today who will go into the goods and services tax in more detail and to explain how it will work-in more detail how it will benefit Canada for many, many years.

subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81-PROPOSED GOODS AND SERVICES TAX
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity to ask the minister a couple of questions about aspects of the goods and services tax that particularly trouble me.
First of all, I think he has taken a bit of the line of his leader in saying, "These people are not allowed to criticize unless they provide a detailed alternative". I would ask him to go back and review the comments that I made. That statement is a form of intellectual dishonesty because we do have an existing tax system in Canada and an alternative has been proposed. If public debate is going to be meaningful on this issue, what we need to do is focus on the proposed alternative and debate that so that Canadians understand exactly what it is that is being proposed. In criticizing that approach he has essentially tried to adopt the strategy, which I am sure he would like, of making the defence and offence.
I would like to ask him about something which truly troubles me about this tax, or two aspects of it. The first is the effect on lower income Canadians. The minister was just referring to the refundable tax credits which are meant to alleviate the amount that this tax is regressive.
If the government is really concerned about ensuring that the tax is not regressive on low income Canadians, why on earth are those tax credits not fully indexed? They are going to erode at 3 per cent a year. These are the poorest, lowest income people in Canada.
Supply
The other aspect of this that troubles me is the effect that it will have on our diverse regions. The manufacturers' sales tax is applied at the manufacturing level. The goods are then transported by and large from central Canada to the extremes, especially the north. The new tax will be applied at the retail level. Therefore, in addition to existing excise taxes, it will result in a 9 per cent tax on the transportation costs incurred in getting goods to the regions, the north in particular, a very significant increase.
When the finance committee was in Whitehorse a couple of weeks ago we heard about how the 25 per cent additional cost-of-living burden is experienced in Whitehorse as compared to Edmonton and Vancouver. This is only going to be made worse when the tax is applied on the transportation included price of the goods. I would like the minister's comments on those two points.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Privatization and Regulatory Affairs)
subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81-PROPOSED GOODS AND SERVICES TAX
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I appreciate those two questions. First of all, on the indexing, as you know the government in its policy back in 1985-86 indexed programs of the government after 3 per cent, with the exception of the senior citizens' pensions which at the time we attempted to do as well. In this particular instance this will follow the policy of the government as stated.
That is not to say that the base level cannot be adjusted from time to time, and is, as the hon. member knows. Even in indexed pension programs and so on and so forth, the base is adjusted from time to time. There is nothing to prevent a government from increasing that base from time to time as is necessary. There is no reason why this will not happen in the future.
For people projecting into 1995 and the year 2000 what this rebate will do based on today's figures is really a little unfair and very hypothetical. As the hon. member knows, governments adjust these bases from time to time, and will continue to do so.
With respect to the second question, everything in the north costs more. It always has. Those people are now paying a 13.5 per cent sales tax which is multiplied upon-they do not know it. It is based on transportation
because-

speakerposition: Minister of State (Privatization and Regulatory Affairs)

speechtext: Excuse me, when an individual buys a product that is manufactured they pay a 13.5 per cent tax on it. They will not do that in the future. As the 9 per cent moves through, the business that pays the 9 per cent on transportation can subtract that from the tax they collect. Therefore, the transportation costs are business input costs and thus can be subtracted. I am the first one to admit that things are more expensive in the north, but a succession of governments has recognized this and has given certain tax concessions to people living north of a certain line that is drawn by the government.

subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81-PROPOSED GOODS AND SERVICES TAX
speechtext: So will you do it?

speakerposition: Minister of State (Privatization and Regulatory Affairs)
subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81-PROPOSED GOODS AND SERVICES TAX
speechtext:
It is there, it is in place now. In fact, because of the resource base which is in the north, the resource industries are going to benefit far more from this sales tax than any others. The overall impact in the north is in fact going to be relatively neutral. I think the Minister of Finance said the other day that it was a 1 per cent difference or something because of the overall impact of the GST.
You cannot look at it on a very narrow basis. You have to look at the overall economy of the region. That is what they did not do when they were making their presentations. I looked at those presentations very carefully, but they did not talk about the overall improvement in the resource industry and the competitiveness of the resource industry, the increase of jobs being created and so on. They did not talk about that.
One cannot look at the GST as did the funeral directors appearing before the committee last night, on a narrow basis. When you are discussing the tax you have to look at the overall economic performance and how it is going to affect the economy of this country. In fact, every economist in this country has said that the goods and services tax is an improvement for the output of this country.

subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81-PROPOSED GOODS AND SERVICES TAX
speechtext: Absolutely not.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Privatization and Regulatory Affairs)
subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81-PROPOSED GOODS AND SERVICES TAX
speechtext:
Check it. We have got figures that show it is costing us $9 billion in production today and that when it is brought in it will increase productivity and increase jobs in this country. That is what this is all about. It is to bring in a fairer, much broader based tax system that in the long run, and even in the short run, is
going to be much fairer to the Canadian taxpayers, and it is going to be much better for our economy. When our economy is working, people are working. When people are working, they are paying taxes. When they are paying taxes, then it is not necessary to increase taxes. You do not have to put heavy burdens on one section of the economy or the other. All they want is fairness. That is what this is all about.

subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81-PROPOSED GOODS AND SERVICES TAX
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I will place my question as quickly as I can to the minister.
Before I do that, I would like to let him know-and he should know this since he is a minister of the Crown- that the manufacturers' sales tax is not part of the resource base industries as he has indicated. The produce and equipment are exempt as it relates to that. You should know that and maybe you should look it up if you get a chance.
Also, if the manufacturers' sales tax is so bad, something which you allude to in your speech, why is it that it went from 9 per cent to 13.5 per cent? Why did it not stay there where it belonged because it is supposedly so bad for Canadians? Please tell us before we retire for lunch why that is so.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Privatization and Regulatory Affairs)
subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81-PROPOSED GOODS AND SERVICES TAX
speechtext: I thank you for that. That is the exact reason why. It is an unfair tax but, at the time, we still needed revenue. The government still needed to operate. We had to pay for health care, post-secondary education, social services the costs of which increase every year. Our grants to provinces are going up every year. They had to be paid for. That is why it went up, but it is not fair. The Minister of Finance was the first one to recognize it. That is why he is trying to bring in a fair goods and services tax that will be fair to all Canadians. Thank you for bringing that point up.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to see that the Commissioner of the RCMP, Mr. Inkster, has officially recognized the importance of reasonable accommodation of human differences. He has recommended to the Solicitor General that members of the Sikh religion who qualify to be RCMP officers should be allowed to wear their turbans, ceremonial daggers and beards.
I also appreciate the justice the RCMP has shown in permitting modifications of the traditional uniform to accommodate female officers.
It is encouraging to see that the RCMP is following the example of the Metro Toronto Police in removing barriers which have prevented equal opportunity for all Canadians to join the RCMP.
I urge the Solicitor General to uphold this progressive and sensible recommendation.

Mr. Speaker, the countdown to possible disaster will begin if the U.S. National Aeronautics and Space Administration goes ahead with the launch of a space probe containing lethal plutonium.
From the moment the shuttle is launched to when the probe, called Galileo, makes two high-speed lowl-level flights over earth, this planet will be in danger of radioactive contamination.
The probe is fueled by 49.25 pounds of plutonium, one pound of which has the capacity to kill every person on earth.
The chance for shuttle accidents is now upgraded from one chance in 100,000 to one in 78. Another launch disaster similar to the Challenger holocaust could release lethal doses of plutonium to be spread by winds throughout this planet.
Because Canada has already been the victim of radioactive debris from a Soviet nuclear satellite, and because one of the purposes of the American space probe is for military reasons, Canada must send a letter of protest to NASA for putting the people of this planet at such unnecessary risk.

Mr. Speaker, the National Library of Canada has recently undertaken a program of mass deacidification of Canadian books. This is necessary because almost all books printed in this century have used acidic paper. However, there are new processes available which allow for the production of alkaline books.

October 12, 1989
S. ft 31
The federal government is a huge user of paper and publisher of documents and therefore it would make sense for the federal government to take the initiative and convert to the use of alkaline paper for publishing documents. Not only would this extend the shelf life of these publications, thus saving money for the National Library, but the reduction in the use of acidic chemicals in paper production would benefit our environment.
This is an opportunity for the government to lead by example and because of the size of its printing operation I believe it would have a major impact.

Mr. Speaker, I rise today to bring to the attention of members the issue of Canada's child care crisis, and that is exactly what it is, Mr. Speaker, a crisis.
At the present time, we have parents who cannot afford child care; parents who cannot find child care for their children; parents who must put their children's names on waiting lists just to get into a child care facility; and we have child care staff who, under the current system, earn less than workers who look after some animals. This is a shameful situation.
Back on August 11, 1988, the Prime Minister said:
We want the best of care for our future generation.
The Prime Minister also said:
This government is committed to social justice for all Canadians.
Child care is the centrepiece of that commitment.
I ask, Canadians ask: Where is that commitment?
At this time, we do not need more studies, reports, and task forces. Canadian families need a national child care plan, one of quality, affordability, availability, accessibility, and they need it now. Children are the only group in our democratic society whose political rights are entrusted to another group. This government is not worthy of that trust. If children were given the right to vote-
