It is imperative that we do everything we can to prevent further unnecessary traffic accidents and fatalities on a hazardous highway which will become more so, as alternatives to it are eliminated.

Mr. Speaker, I rise today to discuss flying the friendly skies of deregulation with general reference to northern Canada.
Our jet service was, or will be, replaced with some smaller aircraft which will provide us with more frequent flights, although some aircraft will have no toilet, no food service, no physical space, no host or hostess, but we can still anticipate less expensive fares because of increased competition. Mr. Speaker, would you believe it is more expensive for anyone to fly Ottawa-Sault Ste. Marie return than it is to fly to Florida, Puerto Plata, Frankfurt, Amersterdam, Paris, Copenhagen, Brussels, and yes, even Casablanca.
The return flight to Sault Ste. Marie is $509. So much for cheaper fares. And let us not forget the unacceptable 9 per cent sales tax. The skies are less than friendly for the people of northern Canada.

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre (Mr. Harb) said not long ago in LeDroit: "In 1984, the Mulroney Government stopped paying municipalities the subsidies that until then helped them absorb part of the costs of infrastructure maintenance."
October 12, 1989

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre should have done his homework before making that statement, because the Liberal Government terminated the subsidy program for local community services in 1982.
We should remember it was the federal Liberals who lost Canada billions of dollars, for no good reason, with their scientific research tax credit in 1983-84.
Mr. Speaker, that is the program the Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre should have mentioned in Le Droit, a program that was cancelled by the Tories shortly after they came to power, a program to which reporter Paul Morisset referred in L'Actualite of February 1987, in the title of his article: The Robbery Of The Century.

Mr. Speaker, as members of the House will know, two weeks ago I arranged for the film, Eclipse of Reason, to be broadcast through Oasis on Channel 98. This film discusses second and third-trimester abortion from the medical point of view and depicts the procedure which is endured by the unborn child. I took this action so that members and senators of all parties would be better informed on the medical facts before entering into debate on this issue.
Although I am well aware of just how busy members are during a session, I hope that all took the brief 27 minutes out of their schedules to watch this short but informative documentary. If, however, members were unable to view the film on one of the three days that it was shown, please feel free to contact me and I will arrange a private screening.
I am certain that with this additional perspective members and senators will be better informed about the emotional subject of abortion.

Mr. Speaker, the problem of drug abuse and trafficking, and together with the vast chain of associative problems, must become a paramount concern of government and citizens alike. Decisive action must begin in earnest to curb this rising tide which overwhelms large segments of our population and costs such exorbitant sums in policing services and health care.
It has been suggested by the Owen Sound Ontario Board of Police Commissioners, and which I agreed to as well, that all profits of assets seized under the Narcotics Control Act and subject to Bill C-61 be returned to the municipality in which the seizures were made. These funds would be directed into drug education and prevention or treatment programs at the local level, a move in the right direction if we are ever to be successful in cooperating to remove this tremendous loss of potential energy and leadership among our population and to lead us toward a drug-free society.

Mr. Speaker, yesterday the Premier of Quebec introduced his new Cabinet. Today, I will not comment on individual appointments. I will let history be the judge!
Nevertheless, I think Mr. Bourassa is to be commended for having asked a large number of women to shoulder some very important responsibilities. At Cultural Affairs, Regional Development, Finance, Communications and Status of Women, they will have their work cut out for them.
Mr. Speaker, the women of this country have taken their place in political life, but above all, they have shown that with their skills, judgment, intelligence and sensitivity, they are able to play a major role in public affairs today. It would of course have been better to hear a man say this. I admit that I appropriated this role with all due humility and, Mr. Speaker, I hope the opposite sex will not hold it against me.

October 12, 1989

Mr. Speaker, on this the day of the Person's Award, a report has been released in Montreal which gives a startling reminder of the pervasiveness of violence against women in Canada. Women in this country live in fear, fear that they will be raped, abused or assaulted on the street, in their homes, by strangers, by friends, or by husbands. Sadly, their fear is justified. One million Canadian women will be abused by their husbands or partners in the next 12 months. One in four Canadian women can expect to be assaulted in their lifetimes, and half of those women will be assaulted before the age of 17.
Fifty-six per cent of urban Canadian women are afraid to walk alone in their own neighbourhoods after dark. Women who have been abused still face a society which considers them to blame, a society that tells them over and over that they do not have the credibility, the money or the power to fight back.
The women in Canada face a government that has yet to take a leading role in stopping the violence that is directed toward them. The government's allocation of $40 million last spring was a paltry attempt at a shortterm fix to a life-long problem.
I urge this government to take a real stand against violence toward women.

Mr. Speaker, one of the most important communities in the riding of Elk Island is Fort Saskatchewan. This city of over 12,000 people was named after one of the first Northwest Mounted Police forts in Canada. Since 1874, the fort on the North Saskatchewan River has served as a symbol of law and order in Canada.
As part of the foundation of the present day Royal Canadian Mounted Police, this community offers much to the history of Canada. Respect for the RCMP with its rich heritage and long-standing traditions is great not only in Fort Saskatchewan, but also in other parts of the Elk Island constituency.
On behalf of all of the people of Elk Island, I salute our police fort community and celebrate the valuable contribution of Fort Saskatchewan to the history of the RCMP in Canada.

Mr. Speaker, the Government of Saskatchewan is attempting to construct a replacement dam in Island Falls in northeastern Saskatchewan without being subjected to a federal environmental assessment and review process.
As was the case with the Rafferty-Alameda project, Premier Devine is saying that he is going to do what he wants regardless of how it affects the province of Manitoba.
Again, Manitoba's Gary Filmon is silent. When the original Island Falls dam was built in the Churchill River in 1927, no environmental review took place. For over 50 years this project has flooded Manitoba Crown lands and Indian reserves. Despite what Saskatchewan is saying, plans for the new dam are very different from the original dam. The dam will change water levels, damage fisheries, wildlife and waterfowl habitats. Navigation and water supply will be negatively affected. The lives of the Mathias Colomb and the Barren Lands band members will be changed forever.
The Minister of the Environment has a duty and he must ensure that a full environmental assessment review process takes place.

Mr. Speaker, on Tuesday, John Wesley Beaver, fondly known as Jack, died in Cobourg after a lengthy illness.
He was a great Canadian, a leader throughout his life, whether as a young man excelling in athletics, winning a middleweight boxing title, or serving his country during World War II as a spitfire pilot in the Battle of Britain and invasion of Europe, or in his professional life as an electrical engineer rising through the ranks of Ontario Hydro to become President and Chief Executive Officer of Churchill Falls Inc. Labrador. Mr. Beaver, a longtime friend, was an Ojibway Indian from the Alnwick reserve in my riding. He was a descendant of generations
October 12, 1989

of chiefs. He himself was chief for four years in the early 1950s. He contributed greatly to his native community, working with it to achieve self-government and to build an economic base through small business on reserves.
His views and counsel will be greatly missed both within his native community and in the corporate world. Our deepest sympathies are extended to his wife Marjory and their children and other members of the Beaver family as we all mourn the passing of this great native Canadian.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. John N. Turner (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, will the real Minister of Finance please stand up?
Oh! Oh!

I do have a question for the Minister of Finance. For five years this minister has refused to provide any money for the treatment of raw sewage by Canadian cities and towns. In that time, during the custody he has had over our nation's finances, more than six billion pounds of raw sewage have been dumped by Canadian municipalities into Canadian lakes and rivers. Let me put this into context for the House.
Last year alone the equivalent of 150,000 drinking glasses full of chloroform, 84,000 glasses full of arsenic and 2.5 million glasses full of lead were dumped by Canadian municipalities into the Great Lakes.
Does the Minister of Finance, after five years reflection, still not think that this dumping of raw sewage into the Canadian environment and into the Great Lakes system is not a responsibility of the Government of Canada? When is he finally going to put in some money to respond to this crisis?

Mr. Speaker, perhaps you would allow me to answer on behalf of the Minister of the Environment.
Oral Questions
What the right hon. gentleman is reciting here is quite an indictment of the municipalities and the provinces which have the principal responsibility for the treatment of effluent from city sewer systems.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader; Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
Pass the buck, is it?
Mr. Oberle Mr. Speaker, it is not true, as the right hon. gentleman asserts, that there has been no action by the federal government.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader; Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: What do you mean, it is not true?

We have contributed to research and information. We have assisted municipalities and provinces in tightening up their regulatory process. The fact remains in the end that the responsibility for the management and treatment of effluent remains with the municipalities and the provinces.

Mr. Speaker, the hon. minister can talk about constitutional jurisdiction. Why do we have a federal Minister of the Environment, why do we have a federal Minister of Health if we are not going to exercise some responsibility at the national level, in conjunction with our municipalities and our provinces, to clean up this mess? He should respond in a more-

Hear, hear!
To get back to my question, Mr. Speaker, although it seems the Minister of Finance once again is either unwilling or unable to answer, every year this Tory Government spends four times as much on advertising as it intends to spend on cleaning up the Great Lakes.
Since we all know that companies will now have to commit billions of dollars to clean up our environment, could the Minister of Finance explain why his 9 per cent tax will apply to pollution control equipment?

Mr. Speaker, we are not surprised at the simplistic solutions that the opposition would propose for the clean up of the environment and the clean up of the Great Lakes. It is the same solution they have used in the past and that is to spread money at the troubled waters. That in itself is not the solution.

Oral Questions
It is not a national priority you are telling us.

Mr. Speaker, if that were a solution the problem would not be as severe as it is today. The fact is that the authors of the report published yesterday admit that much research needs to be done. We do not know what the effects are on health. The fact is that action has been taken. Action committees are under way, studying and working to clean up the hot spots. We have mounted two trusts. One in the area of remedial action and a more important one perhaps in the area of preventive measures that need to be taken in close collaboration with industry, municipalities, states, provinces and government.
Mr. Turner (Vancouver Quadra) Mr. Speaker, the minister is doing a brave job-I say this to the Deputy Prime Minister-in responding to a question the Minister of Finance ought to have answered. He is talking about research. We do not need to research pollution. We need some action in this country. I say to the Minister that he cannot see the forest for the trees on this particular problem.
Mr. Speaker, since the Minister of Finance is not responding, I want to put a question to the Minister of Transport. The final recommendation of the report released yesterday jointly by the Institute for Research on Public Policy in Canada and the Conservation Foundation of the United States reads this way and I quote:
We require sweeping changes in lifestyle from societies
increasingly dependent on the motor car for transportation.
How can the Minister of Transport release at the same time his own absurd, ludicrous, ridiculous and even phoney impact study on the cutting of VIA Rail and say that 2.5 million more Canadians travelling by car every year as a result of the cuts will not be increasing the pollution problem in the country? Where has he been living for the last few years?
On the moon.

Mr. Speaker, I have already tried to explain to the right hon. gentleman the way in which the process has to be worked. I will try again.
First, the law requires the minister responsible to make a preliminary study to see if it is necessary to go forward and go further in terms of environment. The figures here are based on facts. They are there, and the Leader of the Opposition could question all the facts. We have considered the facts which have been proposed by Transport Canada. I should be more specific. They have been totally endorsed by the officers of Environment Canada.
Oh, oh!

The Leader of the Opposition says that it is a phoney document. I am sorry, but I have all confidence in the officers of Environment Canada. I can guarantee that those figures are good. There is no reason, based upon those figures, to go further in terms of the environmental study, and we won't, Mr. Speaker.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, if the study to which the Minister of Transport referred is so reliable, where are the figures on nitric oxide and carbon dioxide? Where are the facts, on acid rain and the greenhouse effect, following the cutbacks at VIA Rail? Why wasn't this kind of study done by experts at the Department of the Environment instead of by the Minister's officials?

Mr. Speaker, everyone except the Liberal Party understands that as far as the VIA Rail network is concerned, it all depends on the number of passengers we take out of the network and put on other modes of transport. We said that theoretically, because some people may take the train, 2,400,000 people would travel by car.
Mr. Speaker, I am happy to say that since the 70's, 96 per cent of hydrocarbon, carbon monoxide and nitric oxide emissions have been reduced, and that by the year 2000, these emissions will be down to 5 per cent. This started under the previous government. Canada has some of the strictest regulations in the world on emissions of polluting substances, and that is the perspective in which the study was carried out. It is in the same perspective that I say to the Hon. Member for Windsor West that this study is a valid one. It shows it is unnecessary to go any further, because once again, its conclusions are entirely endorsed by the Department of the Environment, by officials of the Department of the Environment, and the study states that it is useless to go any further because the consequences are absolutely negligible.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, we have had nothing from the Department of the Environment other than the Minister's silence and absence.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it was reported today that a group of American railroaders want to operate three passenger rail routes in Canada in place of VIA Rail's service which the government wants to eliminate. In fact, their spokesman said: "The public has proven that despite the intentions of the federal government it wants passenger rail service and will partronize it when available".
Why doesn't the government allow VIA Rail to continue to operate these services? Why does the minister and the government show less confidence in Canadian passenger rail service than a group of American entrepreneurs?
Mr. Speaker, because Canadians will have to pay for the deficit that you created. Canadians know increasingly that you never cared about the deficit, but we do care about the deficit.
Hear, hear.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Transport. Canadians have seen in the last 24 hours, whether it comes to the Great Lakes or VIA Rail, in terms of the impact the government is all talk and no action whatsoever.
I want to ask the minister about his so-called environmental impact study. I have three previous studies that have been done. The Fraser-Thompson Corridor, a 100 page document on environmental impact; the Alaska Highway Pipeline, Environmental Impact Study of 100 pages and a third one, done interestingly enough on CN Rail Twin-tracking Program in British Columbia alone-one part of the whole railway system-a 100 page document. In contrast I have here a seven-page mimeographed handout that the minister prepared over the
Oral Questions
weekend. Will the minister now be honest with the people of Canada and admit that his so-called study was a complete fraud when it comes to the environment?

Mr. Speaker, it is obvious again that the Leader of the NDP does not understand. The situation is much more complex than what he raised. I repeat what I said. We took the passengers on the current network who want to be served and we moved those passengers to other modes of transportation.
I will give you, Mr. Speaker, just a little figure which will explain what I am talking about. If you move all those cars on highways, where at the present time we have 142,000 cars moving at the same hour and what if we put on the Canadian highways 142,000 more. I would like for you to understand once again that the figures are good. They are the figures accepted by Transport Canada and Environment Canada.
Mr. Speaker, neither the figures nor the minister are any good when it comes to the environment.
Hear, hear!
Oh, oh!

The minister cannot name a single environmentalist in the country who will support what he has done in the last 24 hours.
With reference to the need for a serious job in terms of studying the environmental impact on the VIA proposal, the Great Lakes study itself that came down yesterday made very specific reference.
I ask the minister to check it out; do not take my word for it. On page 25, they said that if we are going to deal with the Great Lakes we have to deal with the whole ecosystem, particularly air pollution. They cite the need to reduce auto remissions. They cite the need, therefore, for further studies about the impact of alternative modes of transportations on the environment.
If the minister were serious, on the part of the government that claims to be serious about the Great Lakes would he not now admit that in terms of his responsibility on VIA Rail they ought to have done a comprehensive alternative use of transportation study to help reduce air emissions in the Great Lakes region?

Oral Questions

Mr. Speaker, I have two points to make. The first one is that I do not understand when the leader of the NDP asks for a more comprehensive study.
He was laughing at me when I proposed a royal commission to look at the future of transportation. Of course it will consider the environmental side of the new transportation system.
When something is serious it is not for the leader of the NDP. Dealing with the quality of the leader, I will have the elegance not to comment on that.

Mr. Speaker, I am glad the minister reminded me about his royal commission after the fact. That is precisely the point: the government is making a decision now about VIA but is doing its study afterward. The government is supposed to do the environmental study ahead of the project to head off the effect.

Mr. Speaker, the Government refused to conduct a serious environmental impact study on the VIA Rail cuts. The same Government has not taken a serious stand on the Great Lakes.
Would the Minister admit that the only aspect of the environment that matters for the Government is propaganda?

Mr. Speaker, once again I am surprised at the reaction of the New Democrats' Leader, because he claims that the study which was done, and I always said that it was a preliminary study, as required by law to determine the need for a supplementary study- The preliminary study does not require us to conduct a further study. What surprises me, Mr. Speaker, is that this study was endorsed by Environment Department officials, and any comprehensive study called for by the New Democratic Leader would be done by the same Environment officials.
So why are they wrong now and why would they be right if we had a comprehensive environmental study?
Mr. Speaker, a little consistency from that side of the House, please!

Mr. Speaker, in the absence of the Minister of the Environment my question is for the Deputy Prime Minister and is with regard to the Great Lakes water quality.
Canadians are scared and concerned about the massive toxic soup of the Great Lakes. The minister will be aware that many of the remedial action plans announced in 1985 are actually remedial delay plans. Not a drop of water or a grain of poisoned sediment has been cleaned. Canadians want action.
The Prime Minister announced last year $75 million for clean up. Now the minister is saying that it is only $55 million plus $20 million for a health study. If the government is so committed to action, why the delays and why the drop in clean-up funds? It takes billions, not millions.

Mr. Speaker, my hon. friend is quite right. The task at hand is costly and will require some time and serious commitment by all the stakeholders and all the players. It includes the jurisdiction of the United States, the provinces, the municipalities, the science communities and of course the federal government.
Indeed it can be said that it is quite beyond the capacity or the means of any one jurisdiction to address the problem properly. The fact is that the federal government, since 1984, has taken very decisive action. It is not true that nothing has happened.
Everybody here is as well informed as I am about the work that has gone on in the Windermere Basin in the Hamilton Harbour. It is one of the sites that has been identified as one of the hot spots. We now have solid agreements with the jurisdiction in the United States. We have agreements with the provinces. The municipalities are involved. The science community is involved in various ways in the universities that study and do research. Things are in hand. What else would the hon. member have us do?

Mr. Speaker, I have a supplementary question. The Great Lakes Water Quality Agreement has no real mechanisms for putting people's feet to the fire. Nothing is legally binding on the U.S. or Canadian government to follow its plan.

Will this government commit to negotiating a formal Great Lakes treaty, with the Americans, to force both sides to follow the rules and regulations and not leave our citizens' health and well-being to the whims of political promises?

Mr. Speaker, as the hon. member knows we have renegotiated the Great Lakes treaty with the United States. There are teeth in the agreement. Action has taken place on both sides of the lakes. In fact the comprehensive monitoring process that has been launched by these treaty negotiations points out that progress is being made. The problem is not as severe as it was 10 years ago.
That does not give us any great comfort, but the fact is that we are making progress and there is a strong commitment, certainly by this government, to complete the task.

Mr. Speaker, television is the key medium of influence for most Canadians. The new broadcasting bill purports to ensure a Canadian broadcasting policy.
In the light of the country's rapidly changing political dynamics, the new broadcasting bill fails to Canadianize and reinforce Canadian unity.
My question is for the Deputy Prime Minister. Why will this government no longer ensure that the CBC is required in its mandate to contribute to national unity through its programming? Why is this government removing, bite by bite, anything that helps to reinforce Canada?

speakeroldname: Mr. Jim Edwards (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Communications):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Communications
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member is referring to Bill C-40 which was tabled in the House earlier today.
I think on careful examination that the hon. member will find that the CBC's role in national cultural identity is strengthened through the insertion of a new subclause to which I would be happy to draw her attention. I believe it is subclause 3(l)(l)(iii). I am sure that she would be very pleased to read that.
Oral Questions
In addition, the new mandate of the CBC is to foster Canadian consciousness. I am sure that we will hear further from the hon. member as the bill proceeds.

Mr. Speaker, I thank the hon. member for his answer. I think Canadian unity and Canadian identity need more than a little subclause.

Why didn't the Government's new legislation make it incumbent on the CBC to promote national unity? Why did the Government forget its responsibility for reinforcing Canadian unity?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Communications
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the answer is the same in French as it was in English, in other words, the proposed legislation makes it incumbent on the CBC to foster Canadian consciousness.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Transport. A few moments ago he said that the whole matter of environmental assessment is much more complex than my leader would believe.
I want to ask the Minister, if it is much more complex would he not admit that a proper environmental assessment would include the following: relative fuel consumption of various modes of transportation; relative emissions of hydrocarbons, carbon monoxide, nitrogen oxide by various modes and their contribution to the greenhouse effect and ground level ozone; the impact of increased traffic in high density areas; the impact of expanding infrastructures and a route by route environmental analysis of all significant factors?
Would he also admit that his study did not examine any one of those items.

Mr. Speaker, I repeat what I said twice. I said that it is a preliminary study which has to determine what will be the environmental effect on other modes of transportation if we move passengers from the trains. That is the bottom line.

October 12, 1989
Oral Questions
The answer is: it will be negligible at the time. It means that we do not have to go further to determine if the new passengers will create more environmental problem. The answer is no. This answer has been confirmed by environmental specialists.
Mr. Speaker, only the Minister of Transport could tell the country that 1.7 million more automobiles on the roads will not add to the environment.
Oh, oh!

I believe the Minister needs some assistance. I have in my hand a document put forward by the Federal Environmental Assessment Review Office called Federal Environmental Assessment and Review Process, Initial Assessment Guide. It is basically a "how to" to conduct an environmental assessment.
Good idea.

It is available from the Library of Parliament. Perhaps the minister would like to have his staff get it, take a look at it and then decide, finally, that what should be done is a full environmental assessment before any of these cuts are proceeded with. Will he do that?
Mr. Bouchard (Roberval) Mr. Speaker, we know that the New Democratic Party would like to have a full environmental assessment by those people, FARO, those specialists in the environment who already decided that we do not need this environmental study. I am trying to understand but do not try to understand the NDP, Mr. Speaker.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I wish to draw to the attention of members the presence in the gallery of Mr. Cyprien Mbonimpa, Minister of External Relations and Co-operation of Burundi.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I also wish to draw to the attention of members the presence in the gallery of a delegation from Austria, led by Mr. Erich Fidesser, Member of Parliament for the Province of Lower Austria.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of State (Agriculture). Last Friday evening, a major fire caused serious damage in the sheep section of Agriculture Canada's experimental farm in La Pocatiere, in the riding of Kamouraska-Riviere-du-Loup which I have the honour and the privilege to represent in this House. Mr. Speaker, flames devastated the new facilities, finished in 1988 at a cost of $1.4 million. About 700 sheep were lost, all ewes belonging to ten different breeds, which were being used in a major genetics and breeding program aimed at increasing the number of births in sheep. Mr. Speaker, since this experimental centre was the second largest in Canada, my question is as follows: Can you confirm, for my benefit and for the benefit of the entire population of Eastern Quebec, what Agriculture Canada intends to do regarding future use of this research centre? Second, does your Department intend to proceed with the construction-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. Perhaps the Minister could respond.

speakeroldname: Hon. Pierre Blais (Solicitor General of Canada and Minister of State (Agriculture)):
speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of State (Agriculture)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is a very important matter. At the facility, which was a considerable asset to sheep raising in Eastern Canada, we luckily managed to preserve all genetic records. We already have many breeders who will be able to take advantage of our findings. I think that is good news.
As far as rebuilding is concerned, our people are now working on this aspect, and I think we can say the Government intends to rebuild the facilities, Mr. Speaker.

Mr. Speaker, I have an urgent question for the Minister of Indian and Northern Affairs concerning the appalling and unacceptable conditions that exist in a number of the Six Nations Reserve schools, of which he is aware, which I have seen first hand, and which are being boycotted by some 1,200 elementary school children.
October 12, 1989

In 1985 the fire marshals indicated that there were dozens of infractions to fire and safety regulations which needed immediate attention. It took the minister four years to take action.
Will the minister make a commitment in the House today that funds will be made available over and above what he has committed to date to bring the schools up to the proper safety levels? Will he commit to remove instead of just hide the asbestos which has been found in these schools?

speakeroldname: Hon. Pierre H. Cadieux (Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development):
speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would just like to remind my hon. colleague that I have only been Minister of Indian Affairs for about eight or nine months. Therefore I did not have the benefit of those four years he is referring to.
It is an important question, Mr. Speaker, and I hope I will have the courtesy of being able to answer. It is an important situation. It is a grave situation that has been looked into.
The health and safety issues that were raised have been resolved. The inspectors of both Labour Canada and Health and Welfare have been on site and have confirmed that the schools are safe. That is not to suggest that there is not more that has to be done. As a matter of fact I have asked Commissioner Harry La-forme of Ontario to look into the matter with the community, because there seems to be a disagreement right now that we are trying to solve.

Mr. Speaker, the disagreement is broken promises. Mr. Laforme is a fine gentleman, but the fact remains that this government, maybe not the minister, made a commitment to build three new schools on the Six Nations Reserve.
The fact was that one of these schools was to be open by this September. No sod has yet been turned. No other Canadian community would tolerate these conditions for their children and this community will no longer tolerate them.
Will the minister finally live up to his promises, start construction of these schools, meet with the chief which he refuses to do, or is he prepared to continue to put at risk the health and safety of the children of the Six Nations?
Oral Questions

speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext:
First of all, Mr. Speaker, I have not refused to meet with Chief Motour.
There was an appointment that had been scheduled for next Monday which I understand has been cancelled by the chief and not by your humble servant here, Mr. Speaker.
With respect to the construction of the schools, they are planned. They request the participation of the community itself because they will be building the schools themselves. We will be proceeding with construction of new schools as was planned.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans. Tuna fishermen in eastern RE.I. have been led down the garden path by this minister's department. They were guaranteed by DFO officials before the season opened that they would be allowed to fish tuna in Atlantic off Canso, and that any tuna they caught there would count against their home zone quota. Once P.E.I. fishermen arrived in the Canso area and started to catch tuna, the DFO officials changed their tune and told them to pack up and go home.
Could the minister explain to this House why fishermen in my riding were misled by his officials?
Hon. Thomas Siddon (Minister of Fisheries and
Oceans): Mr. Speaker, I am advised that regional officials in earlier consultations with the fishermen of the gulf region did indicate that quotas taken outside the region might be deducted from or be considered as part of their quota within the gulf.
We have had such a successful tuna fishery this year in all of Atlantic Canada, including the areas of Northumberland Strait and Fishermans Bank on which the RE.I. fishermen fish, including the North Lake fishery out of eastern RE.I., landed $500,000 of tuna last weekend, that equity has certainly been ensured. All fishermen are being generously treated in the way this fishery is managed this year.

Mr. Speaker, my supplementary question is for the same minister. RE.I. fishermen were given a verbal assurance by DFO officials that they would be able to fish off Canso this year. In fact their rights were written on the licences they received from DFO.

October 12, 1989
Oral Questions
I ask the Minister the following questions: Why have the rights of P.E.I. fishermen been taken away? Will the minister immediately restore these traditional rights to the P.E.I. tuna fishermen?

Mr. Speaker, there are no rights that are written on licences. In the final analysis we manage the fishery to ensure a fair distribution of opportunity.
I am told that in the Canso area traditionally a small number of P.E.I. based boats fish there, but this year because of the bonanza nature of the tuna fishery a much larger number of P.E.I. based fishermen wanted to fish off the Canso area in a different region.
I repeat, P.E.I. and gulf fishermen have done veiy handsomely this year in the tuna fishery, and last weekend alone $.5 million worth of tuna was landed in eastern P.E.I., because that fishery has been very abundant.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for whoever is acting for the Minister of the Environment today.
Tony Hodge, one of the authors of the Great Lakes great legacy study said on Midday today that his greatest concern is that federal politicians are just reacting to polls, that they do not understand the depth of the problem.
The public does understand. If, for example, it is going to take $40 million in Windsor and between $60 million and $70 million in Thunder Bay for sewage treatment, would the public not understand that $55 million is not going to go very far? Would they not conclude that this government is engaged in cynical propaganda or that this government consists of a bunch of ecological nincompoops?
Both.

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member's criticism and that of the author whom he quotes would perhaps be justified if we had behaved as the opposition does, namely, respond to critical questions like that every time there is an article in The Globe and Mail or The Star.
The fact is that since 1984 and leading up to 1987 significant action was taken. Just two days ago we announced a $125 million program with three tasks attached to it: remedial and preventive, as well as a health study.
Let me quote another author of the report, Mr. David Reynolds, who said: "We, frankly, do not know what all this means to human health". He said: "Little research has been done on the long-term effects of chemicals on the 35 million Americans and Canadians who live in the basin".
There needs to be some advance work done to find out just what the problem is. I have already told them that in the case of sewage being discharged into the Great Lakes it is the principal responsibility of the municipalities which will just simply have to readjust their priorities in terms of the management of their affairs.

Mr. Speaker, I guess the hon. minister does not understand that $40 million and $60 million just does not add up when only $125 million is the total budgeted.
Now, referring to The Globe and Mail, how about the upper Great Lakes Connecting Channel Study that said there should be great emphasis placed on such connecting channels as the Detroit River.
Having read that, as I am sure the minister has, how could he explain the fact that Darrell Pekartz from Environment Canada, meeting with the Binational Advisory Council preparing the remedial action plan for the Detroit River, told them that the Detroit River is unlikely to get funding from this program over its duration. How does he explain that? That is not in The Globe and Mail.

Mr. Speaker, I cannot confirm or deny what one or another official of a Canadian government agency may have said to another agency.
All I am telling the hon. member is that if he examines the record he will find that significant action is taken. A commitment is made by the Canadian government and has been in place. Action is taken in all areas of the Great Lakes and in particular in those areas which fall under Canadian jurisdiction.
October 12, 1989

The fact is, as I said earlier, that the solution to the global problem is far beyond any one jurisdiction either in its regulatory capacity or in its capacity to mount the necessary resources, so we continue to mobilize the combined efforts of all those who have a stake in cleaning up the Great Lakes.

Mr. Speaker, I have question for the Minister of Agriculture and his new-found assistant over there. It is a rather urgent question that I have for the Minister of Agriculture.
I have received many phone calls from farmers both in and outside my constituency who are counting on funds to be made available by the Prairie Grain Advance Payments Act. Not one farmer criticized paying the interest that will be required by Bill C-36. Saskatchewan farmers are willing to pay their share toward reducing our deficit. They want to know when our government will be in a position to provide farmers access to these funds that they so desperately need.

The two new runways proposed for Pearson International Airport will increase noise exposure projections in residential areas in the region of Peel. The minister's

own department produced the NEP forecast upon which the city of Mississauga based its land use policies.

Mr. Speaker, I wish I could return the compliment, but it is evident that this government plans to tax us into submission and then drown out our cries of protest with aircraft noise.

Mr. Speaker, my question is to the Minister of Indian Affairs. Canadian Armed Forces Camp Ipperwash on Lake Huron was seized from the Stoney Point Chippewas in 1942 under the War Measures Act. The government promised to return the land when it was no longer required for military purposes. Today the camp is used for cadets and militia; military personnel use it to store their recreational vehicles and as a summer recreation spot for their families.
My question to the minister of municipal affairs is when will the government return the land to the Chippewas and locate military and cadet training camps on sites that were not seized from their rightful owners?

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would like to advise the hon. member that Camp Ipperwash is being used for very important activities of the Department of National Defence, including for cadets and the reserve. We have no plans to make any changes in the present use of Camp Ipperwash.

Mr. Speaker, my question is to the Minister of Finance. Mr. Minister, you have asked the people of Elk Island and other parts of Alberta to change the manufacturers' sales tax. We want to know what is wrong with the old tax. Can we not just fix it up? What is so bad about a tax on production anyway? Why change it now? Why can we not just keep the old manufacturers' sales tax?

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member is quite right. We have a manufacturers' sales tax and we are proposing to change that. The true reason why we are proposing to change this tax is that it is broken. It is not working. It is a drag on our economy. It is a hidden tax on exports, exports that come from right across the country including the hon. member's own riding of Elk Island. It is also a tax on imports that is one third less than on Canadian domestic production. For all of these reasons it is very important to change the tax.
In the last Parliament there were some proposals put forward to have an adjustment of the existing manufacturers' sales tax. The finance committee of the House of Commons was quite critical of this patch on the old tax. It is for that reason we believe it is important to move to a complete revision of the sales tax system.

Madam Speaker, although Parliament Hill is often well insulated against the sounds of the outside world, I think that if we listened closely we could hear the major rumblings of discontent from the rest of Canada. These rumblings, I would suggest are the sounds of the avalanche of discontent caused by this goods and services tax technical paper and proposed legislation that the government is trying to saddle Canadians with.

October 12, 1989
Supply
The force of those rumblings and the voices of Canadians from across Canada will shake the very foundations of this government, a government that has shown contempt for the people of Canada in the past and in this bill once again thumbs its nose at average Canadians. Canadians have had enough and they will not stand for it. I have received letters from a small smattering of those people from my riding. I am sure all members of Parliament on both sides of the House have had many, many letters. Let me give you a sampling from my riding. A letter from Grand Forks in the province of British Columbia states:
This letter is to protest the implementation of the Goods and Services Tax. This is not the solution to reduce the deficit. I think the Government should control their spending, especially their special-interest spending, and determine their priorities. This could generate a lot more revenue without hurting everyone and creating such havoc.
I, for one, have supported the Progressive Conservative party in the past, but will not continue to do so if you insist on this stupid course.
Another letter from Summerland, British Columbia states:
-the complexity of the proposal boggles the mind. Surely a minister with your resources could come up with a less complicated, and more equitable means of raising taxes. I know that were I in your situation, the first thing I would do would be to reduce spending. Surely that is not beyond your capabilities!
Another letter from Penticton, British Columbia states:
I have talked to many young and old, not one of these persons are in favour of this "tax grab". By adding 9 per cent, I for one will keep a real close guard on my pocket-book, and will buy nothing except the most needed.
Please tell the government, that the majority of Canadians do not make the kind of moneys the MPs do.
Another letter from Penticton states:
Mr. Wilson, you missed the boat on this one. Once again the government has underestimated the durability and tolerance of Canadians-
In the United States I would be considered one of the silent majority. I go to work, pay my taxes, and try to save some money for my retirement without complaining. No more! I am going to do everything I can to stop this horrific tax. I will be joining every organization that is against this tax and use every legal means I have to stop this travesty!
Another letter from Grand Forks states:
We have reached the point of saturation of taxes, whether it be federal, provincial, or municipal - .
Between the high interest rates and our "fair" tax system we will surely join other Third World countries in "the rich get richer and poor get poorer and the middle class foots the bill".
From Oliver, British Columbia, this letter states:
-it is hereby requested that your government take a more common-sense attitude in your efforts to decrease the federal deficit. A most worthy step would be to realize we, the taxpayers and citizens, keep the government operating and it does not bode well when we are asked to take less, while we become painfully aware of your government's excessive spending habits.
A letter from Okanagan Falls states:
-I do think that it could be something for someone to give very serious thought to and maybe sometime, somehow, something MIGHT develop to free the "little guy tax slave" from his oppressors and their idea of getting all that they possibly can for themselves and "friends" all the while in doing so the low income people of this country are pushed deeper, and deeper, down into the muck of poverty. Is equitable treatment for ALL too much to ask, or expect? Whatever did happen to the concept that no one should be expected to pay other than what they were able to pay?
Also I have a letter with respect to the goods and services tax and how it will affect a business person from Penticton who states:
As a former member for 30 years of the Federal Progressive Conservative Party, I must now speak out against the government which I, as a small business person, feel has totally lost touch with the people of Canada.
Those are simply a smattering from the mounds of mail that I have received from my riding and throughout Canada as small business critic on what people in Canada think of this particular technical paper and the proposal of a 9 per cent goods and services tax.
The government has promised simplicity. What did they do? They have snowed under the small business community of Canada. That is emphasized by the Canadian Federation of Independent Business which has insisted that the government go back to the drawing board, scrap the present tax, and get down to some serious thought as far as tax reform goes.
October 12, 1989

The small business community cannot take another kick while they are down. I am from the riding of Okanagan-Similkameen-Merritt where, to be parochial, we have been hit hard by the GATT. We have been hit hard by the free trade agreement in our industries with respect to agriculture. Added to the top of that, our tourism industry, which is one of our largest growth industries in the province of British Columbia and certainly in my riding, has predicted the loss of 400 jobs. Across Canada we are told by the tourist associations that there will be a loss by 1994 of $1.3 billion from the revenues of tourism. That is a loss predicted of 30,000 jobs Canada-wide.
We in the Okanagan-Similkameen-Merritt and boundary areas are dependent on the small business sector. We are dependent on tourism. We cannot afford another kick while we are down. We cannot afford this goods and services tax in that area.
As we travelled across Canada on the finance committee, we heard from restaurant associations that stated they will lose 40,000 jobs with massive amounts of money. We have heard hotel associations representing major hotels state that there will be business losses and business failures in the major centres. We heard hotel associations from smaller communities tell us that they are very price sensitive, that the small communities, the small mom and pop operations are the operations that will go down as failures in today's economic climate created by the goods and services tax.
These people are barely eking out a living now. To kick them while they are down when they are finally rising up from the problems in 1981 is not only unfair, but it is despicable. It is terrible that we have to put up with that in the Okanagan-Similkameen-Merritt and boundary country. In that area we do not need the goods and services tax.
I would suggest to you that not only do we not need it in my riding, but the story is the same if you go to the Yukon territories where they depend on tourism. It is the same in Prince Edward Island where there is an agriculture and tourism base. It is the same in Newfoundland. It is the same on Vancouver Island. It is the same throughout the prairies and central Canada.

We cannot stand to have any further kicks while we are down. We cannot stand it in the tourism industry or in the small business sector. The seniors sector, once again, is an area that will be hard hit. One Voice has told us that they cannot see the goods and services tax going through as it is slated. They are diametrically opposed to the very concept of this because it is regressive. That again hits my riding.
Before I complete, let me just read a small section from a statement by the Economic Development Corporation of Osoyoos and area. Osoyoos is a small border town. The Economic Development Corporation is trying hard to assist that community in the business sector. They state that it is the organizations' hypothesis that the goods and services tax will significantly encourage residents to shop in the United States, therefore, significantly hurting local retail businesses and economy.
I think that for much of the 100 mile corridor across Canada that borders on the United States we have seen the evidence of that over the past three weeks before the Finance Committee. There will be a flood of our economy down into the United States and we in Canada cannot stand for that. We have alternatives, and hopefully I will be asked for some of them during the period for questions and comments.
Canada cannot and will not go along with this goods and services tax the government is proposing.

Madam Speaker, I congratulate the hon. member on his presentation.
This morning we had a press conference where we were calling on all of those people who are opposed to the goods and services tax all across the country to join us in a pre-Hallowe'en rally in front of Parliament Hill at noon on Monday to tell this government about their feelings vis-a-vis this regressive, hidden and inflationary value added tax.

In Belgium, the equivalent to the goods and services tax is approximately 25.5 per cent; in France, it goes up as high as 33 per cent; in Greece, it goes as high as 36 per cent; in Italy, 38 per cent, in Portugal, 30 per cent, and in Spain, 33 per cent.

Does the honourable member think that this government is going to be a lot better than those in Europe and will not be tempted to increase this goods and services tax over the years to reach 20 per cent?

From the studies that I have seen, it is clear that in all the countries that have brought in the goods and services tax, within months of bringing in that tax the rate was increased. The latest example from New Zealand is that it went from 10 per cent to 12.5 per cent.
I think in every case not only have they raised the tax that they brought in originally, but they increased their spending to meet the cash cow effect, so what we have is a situation where the governments spend more as they get it in, and look less at what their expenditures are.
It is undoubtedly a fact that if this is brought in, as is often proposed by some of the government's friends in the manufacturing sector, and we broaden the base, bring in foods, do away with exemptions, and if we lower the rate, it is simply a matter of time before the rate is raised up. I think all of the people who have appeared before us in committee have agreed to this.
The inflationary factor that is involved in any level of goods and services tax, particularly the one at 9 per cent, will probably be double what the government has originally told us. The spiral effect of inflation which the government has not taken into consideration due to increased prices and increases in wage demands will have detrimental effects on all of the economy of Canada with a probable increase in the value of the dollar and an increase in the level of interest rates. We will have total chaos and perhaps a major recession as a result of this.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, when this government came to office in 1984, it was faced with a corporate tax system that was riddled with special deductions, exemptions, and credits. The result was a fast-eroding, federal tax base on the one hand, and a corporate sector that was being given all the wrong economic signals on the other hand. A large part of corporate resources and ingenuity was going into minimizing taxes through a plethora of government incentives. The Canadian corporation had lost its way and in fact had been lured into the woods and up the creek by the former government.
Corporate resources would have been better applied to resolving real corporate problems, such as developing more and better products for existing domestic and foreign markets. Instead, they were induced by the former government to scurry after crumbs in the form of incentives, incentives paid for by the average Canadian. The damage done by this policy to the economy was obvious. Large numbers of ventures failed once the incentives either ran out or became insufficient to support uneconomic businesses and large amounts of public funds wasted on schemes such as the scientific research tax credit-quick flips.
Even more distressing was the fact that these special incentives were so attractive that they mounted year after year, much faster than they could possibly be used. This created a tremendous incentive for taxpayers to create intricate mechanisms and schemes to sell unused tax credits and losses to profitable taxpayers.
The credibility of the tax system was in grave danger as a result of this progressive degeneration. The former government not only encouraged this behaviour, they made it impossible for even the best business people to avoid seeking such devices. The danger was not only that corporations would continue to play an increasingly smaller role in providing their share of support to funding public programs, but that individual taxpayers would react to basically an unfair situation by going to great length to minimize their taxes as well.
It does not end there. Socialist members have often raised the fact that the corporate sector's share of government revenues has fallen over the years. This is only partly true, and to the extent that it is, it has not been due to any shrinking of public responsibility by Canadian businesses as other parties suggest. In fact, as a proportion of corporate profits, corporate taxes have not changed significantly over the last quarter century. What did fall was corporate income as a percentage of total income. The reason corporate income declined in importance is that this sector was led down an unproductive path by the former government.
Our government was, therefore, faced with a fundamental choice in 1984. Leave the basic system in place with all of its structural faults and fast eroding base and offset it with a minimum tax, or go to the very heart of the problem by repairing damage inflicted by the former government and restoring stability to the tax system. We chose the latter and embarked upon a program of
October 12, 1989

corporate tax reform which began with a moratorium in 1984 on that great waste of your tax money, the scientific research tax credit-quick flips. This process continues to this day with the introduction of the large corporation tax in the April 27, 1989 budget.
In between, the more important measures have included the termination of the scientific research tax credit, that fitting example of what the opposition stands for; measures to prevent a variety of schemes to transfer tax losses from non-profitable corporations to profitable corporations, schemes encouraged by the policies of the former government, the reduction of accelerated capital consumption allowance rates across a broad range of capital goods and industries; the elimination of the general investment tax credits which proved to be such a failure in producing real wealth; the reduction of a variety of special purpose investment tax credits; an increase in the rate of taxation of capital gains; the introduction of a corporate surtax; the introduction of put-in-use rules to limit the use of deductions where taxable income is not forthcoming; removal of the inventory allowance; curtailment of the use of the leasing to transfer benefits for accelerated capital consumption allowances from non-taxable entities to profitable firms; and a creditable tax on large deposit-taking institutions.
The benefits of this approach to tax reform have been significant. We now have a broader and more stable corporate tax base which ensures that corporations, and especially large corporations, pay their fair share. In total, these measures will provide well over $2 billion in new tax revenues and will help provide the government with the funds it needs to deliver essential services to Canadians. Just as important, the changes to the tax system have turned the corporate sector's attention back to basic economic fundamentals and away from devising complicated ways to avoid tax. This is critical if our firms are to be able to compete in increasingly tough world markets.
What would the opposition have done? What do they propose? A minimum tax, a tax that would leave the old, inefficient and unfair system in place, and try to cover it up with a mechanism which would be very difficult and complicated to administer. Canadian corporations would continue to pursue complicated schemes to avoid tax and
Supply
then pay a minimum tax as an afterthought. Even worse, this minimum tax would have been an unbearable burden to small and medium businesses just barely scraping by as it is. Inefficiencies and unfairness would have persisted and all Canadians would have suffered.
The right approach is to fix the system, not compensate for it. The right approach is to provide a fair and efficient system of taxation. That is what this government did.

Madam Speaker, I was very interested in the comments of this Conservative member as he tried to wind his way through both a defence of a fair tax system and a defence of his own tax system, which I think is basically a contradiction.
There are two things I would like him to address. Given that this is supposed to be a new and fairer tax system, I am a little curious as to why the government now feels that children and students should be heavily taxed. As we know, everything that a child now buys, under the GST will be taxed. As well, students for the first time in our history will be taxed. Their books will be taxed, their food at the universities will be taxed, and their lessons will be taxed.
One of the interesting contradictions in this system is that when somebody goes to a stockbroker, they do not pay tax when buying stocks, but if they decide their child needs to see a psychologist, they have to pay tax on that. I just do not quite understand why a child psychologist is less important than a stockbroker. Perhaps the member has a better insight as to the fairness in that particular system.
I think that nowadays students, particularly part-time students, cannot raise enough funds and they continue to go to school for five or six years to gain their 15 credits. A lot of them are women who choose to return to the work force, and others are single parents to whom this is an additional expense. Because women usually end up at the low end of the labour market, they earn between $4 and $5 an hour. If they are now going to pay 9 per cent more on everything as students, how many hours do they have to put in just to pay the government? It takes a lot of time, and I do not think the Conservative members have given any thought to the absolute unfairness of taxing children and taxing students. Perhaps the member can show us some insight in the next minute as to exactly what is so fair about this.

Madam Speaker, I think one of the things this government has given a lot of thought to is the $350 billion debt created by the former Liberal government. We have to get a hold on this. The country cannot continue to go on living beyond its means.
The hon. member mentioned the cost to students going to university. Canadians are very fortunate in this country to be able to go to university and pay a small amount of the actual cost of their education that they do. We can only continue to support students going to university and support the wonderful social programs we have in this country if we get our financial situation under control.
One of the fair ways of doing it is the way that 48 countries in this world have done it, including five out of seven countries of the G-7, the largest industrialized countries of the world. The only two countries of the G-7 yet to bring in a goods and services tax are Canada and the United States. The United States is looking at it now. We would like to be a leader in North America, as we have been, in tax reform. To be internationally competitive in the world, to continue to be able to pay for social programs that our government has brought in, to continue to provide these services and balance the budget in this country, we obviously have to increase the revenues to be able to pay for them. The experience in other countries has been that this is a fair system. It is not a regressive system. We have introduced an addition to the program in this country where we will provide tax credits to lower income Canadians, to the extent that those in families with incomes of less than $30,000 will actually be ahead of the game in terms of taxation under this GST system. It is a fair progressive tax and one that will help us reduce the national debt in this country and get this country back on its fiscal feet.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise to join in the debate on the motion by the member for Yorkton-Melville. It is an important motion and I am glad it is on the floor for debate today.
Over the last number of weeks and months the nation's attention and anger has turned to the government policy called the GST, the goods and services tax.
Today, we are debating a motion by the hon. member which calls upon the government to scrap this tax. Earlier in the day, the members of this House were treated to one of the finest speeches I have heard since I have been elected in this House and, I am sure, one of the finest speeches in the last number of years, from my colleague for Ottawa South. He spoke eloquently about the concerns that Canadians have with this very flawed proposal, this veiled attempt at tax reform.
October 12, 1989

This latest Tory tax grab, which has been called the GST, proposes to bilk $26 billion from Canadians' back pockets. The government, before it introduced this particular goods and services tax proposal, and the Minister of Finance said that there would be a few principles underlining the new proposal that would be coming in. He said that the first principle is that it had to be a single-tier system. It cannot be a multi-tier system. He struck out on that count.
What we have now, in the words of John Bulloch from the Federation of Independent Business, is a nightmare on Main Street. This government is prepared to put a piece of legislation before this House that, if adopted, is going to cost the small businessman and woman across Canada up to $7,000, according to one of the estimates, in compliance costs with a system that is going to duplicate an already cluttered sales tax system across this country.
He also said, time and time again, that this new sales tax would be visible. But then he had to stand here in the House and look sheepishly at his feet when he told the House that there was no way that he could make this tax a visible tax. He struck out on that count as well.
He also said that the tax was going to be revenue neutral. He talked about the unfair manufacturers' sales tax that was taking in $18 billion in revenue. He called it a killer of jobs. The motion reads as follows:
That this House advise the Government to scrap a proposed goods and services tax and implement a tax system which is based on the ability to pay and which includes:
This is where it gets interesting, Madam Speaker.
(1)	a minimum corporate tax on profitable corporations;
And we all know that the Budget includes a tax on capital.
(2)	taxation of capital gains income, with the exception of farmland sold for agricultural purposes, small businesses and principal residences;
Madam Speaker, there is already a capital gains tax in Canada.
(3)	the restoration of an inheritance tax on wealthy estates;
What is a wealthy estate and when is it not wealthy, Madam Speaker? That remains to be seen!
However, the Opposition forgot to mention the federal Government's previous experience in taxing estates or, since you are from Quebec, that province's experience in taxing estates. That experience led to a single conclusion, namely that the cost of organizing and administering estate taxes was about equivalent to the amount of money collected.
So on the one hand, they say they want to clean up government finances and cut red tape, and on the other hand the Opposition wants us to hire people to produce more red tape. That is their position!
(4)	effectively progressive income tax;
In 1988, Madam Speaker, Part I of the tax reform provided for three tax brackets instead of ten. In fact, it did even better. It changed everything that was called an exemption. Under the old Liberal regime, two individuals, one earning $10,000 and the other $100,000, both had the same exemption, say $3,000, at the end of the year. For the one earning $10,000, it meant $300 or $400 less tax to pay, whereas it was a saving of $1,500 for the one earning $100,000. At that income level, the tax rate makes a $3,000 exemption worth much more. We took all that out. Now we say: Whether you earn $10,000, $25,000
or $100,000, you will have a $1,000 tax credit. We replaced all two pages of exemptions under the old Liberal regime with tax credits. That makes the income tax system not regressive and benefits low-income families and individuals compared to high-income earners.
You see, Madam Speaker, that is the fourth point; it has already been done.
5) tax provisions which encourage environmentally sound practices.
We see the Opposition's hand in that, Madam Speaker. When you don't know what to do with an issue, you give incentives like the scientific research tax credit. It cost Canadians three or four $billion. Instead of taking money, giving it to company x, which will have to report by deadline y on the amount of money z given for scientific research, they created tax credits, which cost billions.
It is the same thing for the environment, Madam Speaker. It is a measure which gives you no way of knowing in advance who will benefit, to what extent, how and when. That is just like asking the Government to throw money out the window. That is what item 5 of the motion does.
In the last five years, Madam Speaker, this Government has done much more for the environment than the former Government was able to do. The Minister of the Environment continues his excellent work. We will not solve environmental problems with tax measures.

This fiscal policy has done two things. That is what the fiscal policy of these last five years has done.

I said that we cut tax shelters, we cut the scientific research tax credit, we introduced a refundable federal sales tax credit for low-income families in 1986. That was innovative. Since 1986, the amount a family or individual receives annually has doubled and it will quadruple in 1991 with the implementation of the new goods and services tax. Madam Speaker, it is high time we had this kind of debate in the House, and I think the New Democratic Party is to be commended for tabling a motion in the House that gives us an opportunity to spend a few minutes discussing tax reform, a discussion I believe is necessary on a subject that concerns all Canadians. Madam Speaker, we would
of course have preferred to see our amendment accepted by the Chair, so that we could broaden the scope of the debate and get at the core of the problem.
Today, Canadians want to know first of all whether our tax system is equitable, fair and visible, and whether it is truly adapted to the needs of Canadians. In other words, whether it is modem enough to meet the demands of the 90's. We all agree that the system needs restructuring, that tax reform is necessary. That is why we made a suggestion this morning for thorough consultations with Canadians and the provinces, with a view to bringing about fundamental tax reforms in this country. We feel this reform, study or consultation should focus on personal and corporate income tax and on any other tax measures that may be used to pay our debts and enable Canadians to continue to enjoy the services and programs that were developed and introduced many years ago. We would like to see a system that is fair to everyone, that is simple, that is based on the ability to pay-in other words, progressive -, that meets the environmental demands of the day and helps provide for sustainable development. The four themes I just mentioned: fairness, simplicity, ability to pay and environmental demands are themes I think should be discussed across this country, because this is truly a problem that demands our attention.
I admit that the motion before us is concerned mainly with attacking the goods and services tax. In that regard, I will just say that I quite agree it is high time for Canadians to get the message across clearly to this Government: the goods and services tax proposed by the Conservatives is unacceptable in its present form because, we must admit, it meets none of the requirements, none of the criteria set by the Finance Minister himself. I will read those criteria to you! Not only the Finance Minister but also the Prime Minister in the 1988 election campaign said the tax had to be revenue-neutral, that it could not bring in more than the present tax, about $17 or $18 billion. It had to be visible, but it will not be; it will be as hidden as the present tax is. It will have to be set in cooperation with the provinces. It will not be! We know that; the Parliamentary Secretary admitted it himself. It failed, it missed the mark. The provinces left the negotiating table and said: No, your proposed formula is not acceptable. The new goods and services tax meets none of the criteria set by the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance.

"The bottom line is that the GST (the goods and services tax) will not be used to raise the revenues of the Government of Canada." He said that on June 19, 1987, on CTV News. These figures are on the conservative side, because if we are to believe certain witnesses-I have here a letter that says the Federation of Independent Businesses maintains that the Mulroney Government will collect 15 billion more from Canadians. Fifteen billion is fifteen thousand million!
About visibility: we wanted a visible tax so that people will know they are payingy taxes on product*. There will be no visibility, because the government has said: legally, we cannot insist that the tax be visible on the bill.
However, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) promised the House a visible tax. On June 18, 1987, he said: "Sales tax reform will eliminate the hidden tax in the prices consumers pay". It says so at page 7634 in Hansard, but it wasn't true!

They told us there would be federal-provincial co-operation. This has an even more complex and damaging aspect, because the provinces will apply their sales tax on top of the tax imposed by the federal Government. Yet over the past five years the Conservative government has saddled the Canadian population with 31 tax increases. Interest rates have been fluctuating at an alarming rate. Low income Canadians are poorer than ever, the rich are richer than ever!
During the past five years under the Mulroney government, the taxes of a family with two children and an annual income of $23,600 have gone up by 60 per cent. The taxes of a similar family earning an average annual income of $45,000 have increased by 30 per cent, while those of the wealthy earning $100,000 a year are up by 8 per cent. that manufacturers who are making the 13.5 per cent savings on their goods as of January 1, 1990-God forbid if it ever comes into force-must pass that savings on to their consumers. And that is one of the big problems because they won't. They didn't when Jean Chretien reduced the tax from 12 to 9 per cent. The experience of this country is, beware, they do not pass these savings on, they just jack up the price and say that it is part of doing business.
I have to tell people also to beware of the shell game here. The 9 per cent will cost a lot more than the 13.5 per cent even though some of my Tory friends say that they are reducing it from 13.5 to 9 per cent. That is a lie. That is not true. On a piece of furniture-a rocking chair for instance-that is manufactured for say $200 on which we pay 13.5 per cent today-which is $27 tax-when that same rocking chair gets through the transportation network, through the marketing and the store sells it and adds on its profits, it will sell for $400. Well, 9 per cent of $400 is $36, so it will cost Canadians more, not less.
That is why I think it is time for this government to drop the idea of the GST and to come to grips with the real issues. It should ask Canadians what they want in terms of fiscal reform.
