subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S. O. 81-PROPOSED GOODS AND SERVICES TAX
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am delighted to take part in this debate today. The goods and services tax is fundamentally important to every single Canadian, to the future of every Canadian.
We in this Parliament have a responsibility to pass on to our next generation a sound economy, a fair tax, and a country that can hold its own with its competitors in the world. I want to say that we should pass on a debt-free country.

I was going to say that we should pass on a debt-free country. Frankly, while the goods and services tax is going to help in this regard, we are saddled with that huge debt we inherited in 1984. The member said we have doubled the debt. Perhaps it has doubled but it is the service cost of that debt that has generated all of the present debt. That government set a pattern that we are having difficulty breaking away from and we are saddled with that huge debt.
In the short time that I have today I would like to talk about why we must replace the existing sales tax. We know that the existing sales tax distorts business, it is hidden from consumers. The hon. member from Vanier was talking about the hidden tax. I would dispute that this new tax will be hidden because, indeed, every single business that will buy must have it separated. This tax will be visible.
The problem with the old tax is that it is hidden. It penalizes Canadian producers. What a terrible thing to have to continue, and the opposition is not suggesting any other way around it. It is very complex. It is unreliable because people can make business decisions to get around the tax.
In 1984 we set down an agenda for economic renewal. The agenda for renewal spelled out in plain terms our government's priorities and principles, and described a clear policy framework directed toward job creation. And what a record we have. One and a half million more Canadians are working now than there were in 1984. The agenda described economic growth, sound fiscal management, economic efficiency and improved international competitiveness.
The plan focused on a strong private sector as an economic leader, on a compassionate social policy to help Canadians in need and on government being a creator of solutions and not one of the problems.
The goods and services tax is the result of extensive consultation and careful study that began way back with the White Paper on tax reform in June of 1987. Tax reform was to be implemented in two stages. In 1988 the government reformed its personal and corporate tax systems. The goods and services tax is the next step in this overall plan.
We are living today with a federal sales tax that was put in place in 1924, 65 years ago. How many changes have occurred in the industrial world since then? Then it was
Supply
simple; manufacturers made the article and wholesalers sold the article. Now everything has changed except our tax. The world economy has also changed around us and Canadians have to change in order to meet the competition.
Today's business world is different. This difference has been recognized by nations around the world. Other nations have changed their tax systems. In fact, 48 nations in the world presently use a tax similar to the goods and services tax that this government is proposing. This is hardly a new invention, hardly something different that we are proposing here today.
The opposition would lead us to believe that Canadians are not able to handle the degree of complexity in the tax, but other nations in the world can. I do not believe that for a moment. I know that Canadians can indeed understand the tax if they are given a chance to understand it and they will, in fact, be able to work competitively in the world.
It has been clear to me for some time that many people, including the opposition, do not understand what is in this tax. In fact, from what I have heard today I know that is true. If opposition members meet constituents who do not understand it as well they do not care. They are quite happy to allow the misconceptions to continue in the constituent's mind. They are not trying to tell them the facts about the tax. They have not studied it.
The member from Dartmouth said "Study the tax". He said there is a 9 per cent tax on bait that can never be recovered. Every business in Canada can be taken to a tax free position through the application of the goods and services tax, even fishermen who pay a tax on their bait.
We have heard from the member from Vanier about the new goods and services tax being a tax on tax, that the Ontario tax will be a tax on the goods and services tax. Indeed, it might. I would like to make two comments. First, the leaders in the provincial world thought they would force the Government of Canada out of this particular field and not let it have a consumer tax simply by not co-operating. I am sure that the citizens of Ontario particularly-I will not speak for the other people across Canada-would want the two taxes. Indeed, the province and the Government of Canada will come to an agreement so that we will indeed have a joint tax down the road.

October 12, 1989
Supply
The member for Vanier also talked about the impact on the lower-income family. He did not bother mentioning the tax rebates that will go to these people and, indeed, give them more money when they are done than what they have at the present time.
Getting back to my topic, which is basically the federal sales tax, items that we buy every day are taxed right now. They include cosmetics, garbage bags, children's toys and kitchen utensils. Even food carries an impact of the federal sales tax. Other things in business such as office furniture and tools carry tax, even though many of those are supposed to be tax exempt. But there is an impact of federal sales tax that carries through in the cost of every single item that is made. It is there as a hidden aspect, but there as well as an added item at the end after manufacturing.
We should talk a little about who pays the present tax. It is suggested by many-perhaps not today for I have not heard anybody say it-that all the tax will come from the consumer. Consumers have forever paid the tax that is built in as a business expense. Indeed, if they pay the tax now, they will pay the tax later.
We have heard them say that the new tax will be 9 per cent on everything, like a tax increase. The truth is it will be very difficult for members opposite to show me any single item that will have a net increase of 9 per cent because there will be cost reductions. There will be competition in industries all over. There are businessmen on this side of the House-perhaps there are not too many over there-who know that competition does keep a lid on prices and will force the passing on of any savings.
The $17 billion in taxes that we collect right now are buried so deeply in production processes that they are virtually invisible to the majority of Canadians. Under the present tax we are taxing the business inputs of our companies which compete with companies around the world. This puts our companies at a distinct disadvantage, both here with respect to the price of products that we sell at home against imported products, and also against selling in other parts of the world. This unfairness in the tax is costing us jobs.
Let us be realistic. What country in the world would let a tax continue that shoots itself in the foot, that hurts itself in jobs and production? I do not think you can find
many others, or any others, certainly not nations of equal industrial growth and ability like ourselves. We are committed to a better future for our children. Any member of Parliament representing constituents in the House should be supportive of such a move to preserve our current good life.
There is another negative aspect of this tax. Manufacturers can organize themselves to evade the tax. They can set up a manufacturing base and move all of their costs and future costs into another company to reduce the amount of tax that is applied to the manufacturing cost. So the present tax is not reliable.
This tax is supposed to cover some 75,000 firms, but indeed it is made very complex because there are 22,000 special arrangements with administrative interpretations. There is an increasingly larger number of court cases which are trying to define the tax as it stands now and show it will not produce the revenue that it does in the future because of this type of organization.
The goods and services tax will apply uniformly across a broad base of goods and services. The present tax applies only to 30 per cent of the products that are sold. This is a very narrow base on which to have a tax which is really, in its own right, a consumption tax.
It is certainly a great understatement to say that the present sales tax is inadequate. It is outdated. It is damaging our ability to compete in the world.
I see that I have come to the end of what I might say. Perhaps I diverge a little too much on the things that the opposition members have said.
Our government has faced and will continue to face economic challenges so that we can ensure Canada's prosperity in a competitive, ever changing world. We have a plan for meeting the challenge ahead. The plan is working. The goods and services tax is an essential part of that plan.

That cash flow problem is going to be increased by 9 per cent. Would it not make much more sense not to have this tax in place and to be more competitive right from the start?

Madam Speaker, perhaps the hon. member does not realize that every manufacturing institution in Canada and the United States will indeed be tax free. There will not be any tax carried on.
He speaks about cash flow. He and I have a kindred interest in farming. That is one area in which I agree there will be forever a claiming back of rebates. Beyond that, in businesses where all products are taxed there will be a positive cash flow because each business will forever have money owing to government in its bank account and will indeed have more money and more interest generated from it.
Products entering from the United States will be as cheap as they are now. Because we compete on the market there, our products will be cheaper. In any case, a 9 per cent tax will be paid on both sides of this issue, imported and on Canadian-made products. It will be applied fairly, which I am sure is what the hon. member must want.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise in support of this motion today. It is a far-seeing motion that is part of real tax reform and which provides the alternatives that the Prime Minister has been calling for. Here are part of the alternatives to real tax reform.
I support this motion not just in support of my riding but in support of the people of Canada-the rights of the people of Canada to be free from a regressive tax grab and to see what real tax reform could look like.
First, I would like to make some comments on the manufacturers' sales tax which, as the previous speaker said, is an unfair tax. I would ask why this Tory Government raised an unfair tax from 9 per cent to 10 per cent to 11 per cent to 12 per cent to 13.5 per cent. In other words it raised this unfair tax since 1984. We can only take from that that in order to deal with an unfair tax this government has decided that it will make an unfair tax more unfair for every Canadian, whether it is to buy their children's clothes, a postage stamp or to bury someone. This is a tax that goes beyond the grave as well.

Supply
We have heard a lot today about the effects of this tax on various ridings. I would like to make a few comments today on the effects on those Canadians who live in our northern regions.
First, it is known that it is vety expensive to live in the northern regions of our country. One of the issues I would like to address about this tax is the potential effect on inflation, which the government itself acknowledges. There will be an inflationary aspect to this tax, some 2.5 per cent according to the government, but to other analysts it will be beyond 3 per cent. There is no tax rebate, no tax credit to compensate northerners, farmers and those who are living in poverty for the inflationary effect of this proposed tax.
I would like a northern resident to say that the cost of living in the north ranges from 25 per cent to 50 per cent higher than southern regions, and in some remote areas in the Northwest Territories it is as much as 75 per cent to 100 per cent higher. We are going to see a situation where residents of northern areas suffer not only from the inflationary effect but also from the tax itself.
As you know, Madam Speaker, many of our goods- virtually all of our goods-from food to processed goods are trucked in or flown in. Northerners are going to be hurt particularly by the added transportation costs when the tax comes on to transportation as it is proposed. This will affect not only those of us in northern Canada, the Yukon and the Northwest Territories, but all northern parts of the provinces and indeed all rural areas which are reliant on these forms of transport. Of course, cutting VIA Rail will be another severe blow to those areas that have relied on the rail system for delivery of those goods.
The 9 per cent means that we will be suffering greater tax hardship than our counterparts in the south. I want to give some specific examples of that. For example, based on Statistics Canada data it is estimated that the average family in Whitehorse, in my riding of the Yukon, will pay $500 more per year than a southern family with the tax increases. Whereas the average Canadian family may anticipate a tax increase-and it is a total tax increase of $2,000 a year-a northern resident can anticipate an increase of approximately $2,500.
Another increased cost to northerners will be the taxes mentioned on transportation. Northerners travel more. They have to, not just to visit family and friends but for medical reasons and to do business. For example, the average Yukon family spent $662 on air travel in 1986 compared with the Canadian average of $211. That is almost three times as much. I want to remind the House that that amount is for essential services which include medical care, business reasons and so on.
What the GST means is that this family will pay an average of $40 more as compared with a southern family on increased air fare alone.
As everyone knows-and even the Hon. Minister of Finance knows-it is much colder in the north. It is much darker in the north beginning this time of year. Therefore, we use more oil, electricity and natural gas, as do other Canadians, but we use more of it than do other Canadians. In Whitehorse the average resident spends $638 on home heating fuels alone. That is compared with some $400 for the rest of Canada. Nine per cent of $638 obviously is more than 9 per cent of $425.
This tax will cost northerners more. This tax is a penalty for people living in our northern regions.
Let me make it clear that I do not in any way support this tax or this form of regressive taxation. That is why I support the New Democratic Party motion which proposes real alternatives and real tax reforms.
I was interested to hear during the hearings of the committee in Whitehorse one of the government members of the committee propose that there would be an adjustment made to the northern benefits allowance to compensate for the increased burden of taxation which may fall as a result of this proposed goods and services tax. I would certainly be interested in hearing more details on that as we have found with the northern benefits tax, which I know is under review at the moment, there are still many loopholes. There are many problems with people in claiming the benefits that they are entitled to under that format.
Northerners know that this tax is unfair, not just to them but to all Canadians. The biggest problem, as I said, is that this is a regressive tax. It is tied to the amount of money people spend and not to their wealth or incomes.
October 12, 1989

Clearly the poor are going to be hit harder by this increased consumption tax. It violates the principle of taxation according to ability to pay. It continues to shift the burden from the large corporations to the consumer.
There are alternatives, and we mention some in our motion. I would like to add a few.
There must be a comprehensive restructuring, as I have said and as we indicate in our motion, of the tax system. For example, there should be an annual net wealth tax. People should not be taxed strictly on their income but on what they own. Net wealth is the best measure of an individual's ability to pay. There are estimates that this could bring at least $1 billion in revenue to the government.
The former speaker talked about the deficit. As we know, a decrease in interest rates of 1 per cent would immediately add $1.6 billion in revenue for the government. Clearly, the calls for a decrease in interest rates-a call by all Parties on the finance committee- could be a measure which could result in an increase in tax revenues as well.
We can limit as well corporate interest deductibility. As I said earlier, with the goods and services tax there will be a tax on stamps and on children's clothing, but there are to be no taxes on the interest on the money that large corporations borrow for mergers and takeovers or, indeed, on any merger or takeover. Stockbrokers are free from having to pay the tax. I think it would be of small consolation to a single parent trying to raise a family and trying to pay for housing to know that stockbrokers' transactions will not be part of this taxable system.
We can raise income tax for the highest earners. The latest statistics already indicate that the luckiest Canadians are those who make over $125,000 a year because they are still those best favoured by our tax system.
We can also eliminate the $100,000 tax free capital gains exemption, except for farms, family businesses and private residences, which would bring in some $600 million in government revenue.
Protection of the environment is the number one issue today. I have seen nothing that indicates that the government has done an environmental assessment of
Supply
this proposed goods and services tax. What will this mean for the purchases of environmentally-friendly products?
An environmental tax on the other hand would work toward solving two problems-protecting our environment and creating tax revenues. We need a genuine minimum corporate tax.
These are just a few of the suggestions for tax reform. What this government must realize is it cannot continue to shift the burden on to the poor and middle-income earners. It cannot continue to have support from the Canadian people. It cannot continue to call this tax reform.
Madam Speaker, today we are proposing some elements of real tax reform. I urge all members of this House to support this motion.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I appreciate having an opportunity to speak on this motion, especially as someone who has spent the last three weeks hearing representations from people both here in Ottawa and in other parts of the country.
I notice that this motion essentially calls upon the government to abandon its efforts to reform the federal sales tax and to do other things. I would say that unfortunately it appears that the members who are proposing this motion have not been listening to the groups which have been coming and speaking before the finance committee.
Quite frankly, what I can tell you and other members of the House who may not have been free from their other duties to come and observe all of our committee meetings is that, for the most part, about nine out of ten groups that have come before the committee have endorsed the concept of a value added tax, or a goods and services tax.
In almost every case they have had particular measures that they want changed or done differently. We can look at small business, for example. Mr. Bulloch spoke on behalf of small business. He said there was no other solution to the problem but a type of goods and services tax. He was unequivocal about that. He wanted the provinces to be part of the system so that there would be one system in Canada rather than two, but he had no doubts about a value added tax.

October 12, 1989
Supply
We had a representative from the National Council on Welfare, Mr. Ken Battle, who came and told us that the proposal put forward by the government is superior to the system that is in place today, a system, I might add, that has been there since 1924. He had some concerns with regard to the credits and the indexing of the credits, but comparing the proposal to the existing system was a positive step. I would have thought that the New Democratic Party might have been interested in hearing from the National Council on Welfare.
We had, in addition, Mrs. Shirley Carr, who came before the committee on Tuesday morning representing the Canadian Labour Congress. When I asked her directly how she felt about a value added tax which is in place in 48 other countries in the world, she said she had no difficulty in supporting the concept of a value added tax. Again, she had some concerns about this particular proposal and wanted some changes. Effectively, she wanted us to go back and have a royal commission to see what we could do in that regard.
Maybe I should speak on that for a moment because I think some people have the impression that what we are doing is somehow new or just thought up in the last few months or a year. In fact, the existing federal manufacturers' sales tax has been around since 1924. Today it accounts for about 20 per cent of the revenue of the federal government-around $18 billion. It is a large number we are talking about, but a system that has been in place for many years.
However, almost since the time it was brought in, its flaws have been known. There have been a variety of commissions, studies and examinations saying we have do something about this. In 1940, 50 years ago, there was the Rowell-Sirois commission which examined this issue and came to the conclusion that something should be done. In the 1960s there were various studies. In 1966 the Carter commission, which has been referred to by other members, examined taxation in Canada and put forward some suggestions. On the income tax side, those suggestions were adopted in 1971 by the then Minister of Finance, Edgar Benson. However, the government did not proceed with the other part of the equation, that is sales tax reform.
In 1975, we had the Minister of Finance of the day, who is now the current Leader of the Opposition, Mr. Turner, put forward a paper on the subject, seeking to reform the federal sales tax system. Of course nothing happened. Any time that previous government over the last 20 years before this government took office ran into some difficulty or some criticism it abandoned the effort. So that was abandoned. Mr. Turner abandoned it.
Mr. MacEachen tried to resurrect it when he was Finance Minister in 1981. Mr. Lalonde did the same thing by putting forward a proposal to reform the federal sales tax system. He then appointed a commission called the Goodman Commission which studied that particular proposal. It came to the conclusion that that was not particularly very good, and that it should look to something more along the lines of what we are doing now. Mr. Bulloch spoke about that series of commissions because he was a member of that commission. That is why he was able to state unequivocally that really the only answer is some form of value-added tax.
With all that support and with all those studies for 50 years it seems to me that now is the time to act-no longer talk about it, no longer study it, no longer have any more commissions and studies. Act. Put a proposal on the table. That is what the government has done.
I am not entirely satisfied with the proposal of the government. I will be the first to say that. I favour fewer exemptions, a broader base and a lower rate. I will still say that the proposal on the table by the government is superior to the existing system. While I will seek some changes along the way, especially in my role as a member of the finance committee, I know that one thing we cannot change is not doing something at all. We must proceed in some fashion.
For this motion to suggest that we do not proceed on the subject is I think, frankly, totally misguided. It does not recognize what 50 years of history has taught us. It does not recognize what individuals have been telling us.
The issue of farming was raised here a few moments ago. I should mention that last week we heard from the Canadian Barley Growers, the Canadian Wheat Growers and the Canadian Cattlemen, among other farm groups. We also heard from Unifarm. Every one of those groups endorsed a value-added tax. They said that, first, they would like a lower rate but that in order to get the lower rate they would like to be part of the system which would make food taxable.
October 12, 1989

Not only did they endorse a value-added tax, or a goods and services tax, they said that they should be brought into the system as well.
I recognize that people who have been reading newspapers or seeing clips on television may have got somewhat of a different impression. Those clips focus on the negative aspects that a particular group wants to raise when it comes before the committee. It is up to us to hear a group to try to do what we can while maintaining the integrity, over all, of the proposal.
The alternative suggestion that the New Democrats are putting forward deserves some examination here. Their first point is that there should be a minimum corporate tax on profitable corporations. That is fair enough. I think one of the problems we have is that they suggest and continue to quote numbers about there being 89,000 profitable corporations.

speechtext:
A new number we have had recently is 89,000. Somebody has put that number forward. In any event, there are not that many corporations to begin with. If we were to take a definition of "corporation" commonly accepted under the Corporations and Labour Returns Act there are about 2,000 corporations that could be classified as large, profitable and unprofitable.
When we had a study examining those corporations that do not pay tax even though they make a profit-the study is available in case people have not had an opportunity to see it-we found that the largest group that falls into that category includes farmers and small business people .The reason they fall into that category is that they have very cyclical incomes. A farmer may have a large crop one year and no crop the next and then another crop. In any given year he may appear as a person who had a reasonably sizable income. He paid no income tax because for the previous two or three years he had losses. Farmers are allowed essentially an averaging mechanism. The same is true for small businesses. That is why when you talk about a minimum tax and and you talk about profitable corporations that pay no tax the largest number by far is that of farmers and small businesses.
Supply
As long as we recognize that and if we want to increase the tax on that group then that is fine. The New Democrats should say that and be up front about it.
We talk about some other things in here, for example, taxation of capital gains and the restoration of inheritance tax. I am not going to go into detail on those, but I would suggest that if we were to take all the suggestions put forward here by the New Democratic Party in its motion today, we would have perhaps $2 billion, $3 billion or $4 billion available in taxes. That should not be disregarded. That is an important number. But it is nowhere near the $18 billion being brought in today by the federal sales tax. Therefore, this is not an alternative at all and should not be regarded as such.
Their fourth point about tax provisions which encourage environmentally sound practices is interesting. I must say that if there is anything at all redeeming about this particular motion it is this one clause which mentions that. I have said on occasion that we should consider possibly looking at how we might put into the taxation system some elements of a tax, if you like, on polluters or pollution, where we could try to address the issue of the environment in an economic way. If they had more suggestions in this area that might be a motion which I and some members of the House might be able to support.
However, given what they have said here it is not possible. It would not solve the problem. It leaves the entire question unaddressed, even after 50 years of studies, and proposes really no alternative that would in any way try to address the problem that we are trying to address. For that reason I and other members of the government will have to vote against this motion.

This is what that member of the New Democratic Party had to say: "As much as I will fight it and talk about it, between now and the time it is implemented I still want to urge the government to restrain itself in its temptation to give exemptions. Exemptions will not make it more fair. Exemptions will make the tax more difficult to administer. Exemptions will be of greater benefit to those who have more money than to those who have less money. My question is with reference to a statement that was made by the finance minister on a number of occasions prior to the last election and during the election, that is that value added taxes will be revenue neutral.
Lately, over and over again we have been hearing about the impact the goods and services tax would have on the deficit, implying that it would reduce the deficit.
Could the hon. member tell the House how a revenue neutral tax could have an impact on reducing the deficit when it is revenue neutral? If in fact it is not revenue neutral, would the hon. member persuade his colleagues on the government side to come clean with Canadians and say that it will be the cow that we are going to milk over the years in order to reduce the deficit.

subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S. O. 81-PROPOSED GOODS AND SERVICES TAX
speechtext:
I would be pleased to respond to that question. The reason why a person can talk about a tax as being revenue neutral and talk about the deficit at the same time is that the existing federal sales tax is essentially withering away.
One of the problems with that tax is that it is applied in quite an unfair and arbitrary manner, which has spawned a great many court cases. Right now there are approximately 130 cases within the system which are basically unravelling the existing federal tax system.
If, for example, we were to stop proceeding with this and say that we were going to stay with the existing tax system, we anticipate a loss in the order of about $2 billion in revenue immediately, from just what is in the system right now in terms of people challenging the system or reorganizing their businesses basically to shift away and avoid the tax. We would have a $2 billion loss immediately and further losses over time as business continued to move away from the system.
Another thing I could remind the member of is that the manufacturing sector or the goods sector of the economy is becoming a considerably smaller part of the economy than what it used to be. In 1961 it was 63 per cent of the economy. It is now about 53 per cent. So as that sector continues to shrink and the tax base continues to shrink, the rate must be raised on what is left to get the same revenue.
October 12, 1989

In order to maintain the revenue that we are currently getting today, or the same level of revenue, we have to make these changes to preserve the integrity of the system. That is why we can say that it is an important element in terms of maintaining our control over deficit reduction, as well as say at the same time that it is budget neutral.

subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S. O. 81-PROPOSED GOODS AND SERVICES TAX
speechtext:
I am speaking on the NDP motion that would ask the government to scrap the goods and services tax. In order to put it in perspective I would like to go back for a few moments, for my own benefit and for the benefit of some of my colleagues, to make a thumbnail sketch of precisely how we arrived at this position with respect to the goods and services tax and to give you some indication in my opinion as to why the government has had to resort to this measure.
We have to go back and examine why we have taxes. The classical definition of taxes is: compulsory payment by individuals and corporations to government, levied to finance the government services, to redistribute income, and to influence the behaviour of consumers and investors.
It goes back to the Constitution Act, 1867 which gave Parliament unlimited taxing powers and limited those of the provinces to direct taxation. The federal government, under this act, was responsible for national defence and economic development which was extensive back then. The provinces were responsible for education, health and local matters, which then involved only modest expenditures. For more than 50 years customs and excise duties provided the bulk of federal revenues. By 1913 they constituted over 90 per cent of the total.
To finance World War I, in 1917 Parliament introduced personal income tax, corporate tax and in 1920 the manufacturers' sales tax and other sales taxes.
The Canadian tax structure changed profoundly during World War II. In 1941 direct taxes accounted for more than 56 per cent of the federal revenue, and the provinces received grants and the yields from gasoline and sales tax that increased substantially over the years.
Supply
From 1947 to 1962 the provinces with mounting reluctance accepted federal grants as a substitute for levying their own direct taxes. In 1962 this changed again and the federal government reduced its own personal and corporate income tax rates to make room available to the provinces. Between 1962 and 1977 the provincial share of income tax revenues increased significantly.
A tax system, I believe, is judged on a number of factors. We could spend the rest of the day discussing these factors, but I think it is safe to say that the major criteria are equity, efficiency, economic growth, stabilization, and ease of administration and compliance.
What it boils down to is that individuals should be taxed on their ability to pay or, as it was put by Mr. Kenneth Carter in the royal commission report on taxation, appointed in 1962-and his report was in 1966-fairness should be the foremost objective of the taxation system. The poor should not pay more than their fair share, and the rich should not be allowed to avoid taxes through various loopholes.
In 1986 the Conservative government, stampeded by the extensive tax reforms under way in the United States, announced plans to proceed with a comprehensive reform of the Canadian federal tax system in order to keep our tax system competitive with that of the United States. Their intentions, as stated, were to broaden the income tax base to enable a reduction in personal and corporate taxes, and the sales tax would be replaced by what was referred to then as the business transfer tax that was to be a broadly based, value added tax system in which the value added to a product would be taxed at each stage in the production process.
The big objective was to lower tax rates and in particular to reduce reliance on the personal income tax by improving the revenue balance between personal income and other taxes. A simplified tax system was expected to be the offshoot of all these plans, and this would all combine to stimulate economic growth. It sounds good on paper.
What had really happened, I would suggest, was that in the first few years after the Tories were elected they began to worry. Taxable corporate income had been eroded by a sea of losses, investment credits, capital cost allowances, and other tax breaks. The manufacturers' sales tax eventually applied to only one-third of the goods and services sold in Canada because many had won exemptions through legislation and tax decision.

Supply
In other words, a tax base was developing that had become dangerously narrow. Increasingly, the personal income tax was left to carry the weight and rates were being pushed progressively higher and higher. I think we all know in this House that Canadian tax revenues come mostly from three places: corporate income tax, personal income tax, and sales tax. When too much dependence is placed on one of these three the tax system goes berserk and it starts to collapse.
There is no magic mix, but let us look at the record. In 1965 corporate income tax accounted for 20 per cent of federal revenues; personal income tax, 30 per cent; and sales and excise tax, close to 40 per cent. In 1987, 22 years later, corporate tax had gone from 20 per cent to 11 per cent; personal income tax had gone from 30 per cent to 47 per cent; and sales and excise tax was 20 per cent.
As I suggested earlier there is general agreement that there is no magic formula. What you do is you take action, you monitor, you adjust, you watch international competitive trends, and you ensure that there is minimum damage to the economy.
The finance minister's advisers seem to have a sense of mission in which the only prescription seems to be to raise more taxes while the government continues to grind to a certain extent on the expenditure side. We look at the 72 per cent increase since 1984 on personal income tax and, if we do not get some Tory back-benchers to vote against Bill C-28, we are going to have about 90 per cent by 1991.
The Tories don't seem to want to offend big business, so whose left? It is the little guy. To make matter worse, they are also concerned that the gap in corporate tax rates between Canada and the United States is causing a revenue drain. Multinational companies can shift taxable profits to the United States while maintaining deductible expenses in Canada.
The estimates are that for every percentage point of the goods and services tax Ottawa will reap between $2.5 and $5 billion. We do not know exactly. This means that the tax will raise between $22.5 billion, at the very least, or it could raise as high as $27 billion. I think all of us in this House have heard figures greater than that. We have a windfall of between $4.5 billion and $9 billion per year.
That could be reduced for a number of reasons or it could be increased for a number of reasons.
This tax is a dream of this government because it will be less visible than income tax and it will be difficult to evade. It is also a revenue money machine that can easily be adjusted to maximize political benefits.
For example, if the goods and services tax were set at the 24.5 per cent, as it is now in Sweden, the Tories could abolish their federal income tax for individuals and still collect about the same revenue. If it were set at Britain's rate of 15 per cent, they could half all the income taxes.
If we look at the $9 billion that may be a windfall, the income tax could be reduced next year or the year after the introduction of GST by 15 per cent. Guess who is going to look like the good guys? Guess who is planning to look like the good guys? I am suggesting that the Tories are hoping to avoid this measure as their death-knell and they are hoping to turn it into trump card.
Let us have no illusions. Every tax has a natural history. It begins with a wide base and a low rate, but as demands for special treatment grow louder the rates inevitably rise and the base narrows. I am just waiting for the Prime Minister say: "Watch me".
I opened my presentation with a serious definition of taxes. I would like to close with another. Ihxes have been defined by some as a method used by the government in power to artificially induce the rainy day everybody has been saving for. Is this really what the government is doing? I am not prepared to watch this, neither are my colleagues on this side of the House and I would suggest over there. I hope that there are some of my colleagues from across the House who are going to say the same thing. The Canadian people will not accept this, and we are going to fight and fight to make sure that we do not see it pass.

subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S. O. 81-PROPOSED GOODS AND SERVICES TAX
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, that is what it was intended to accomplish.
I think it is only natural that Canadians, probably every one of us, will dislike a new tax program of any kind. I do not see us out to sell Canadians on a goods and services tax or any other kind of a tax program, but rather I believe that most Canadians are honest, intelligent, responsible people and they can be persuaded to accept or even to support a new tax program if it makes sense and if it is necessary to achieve our objectives as a nation. That is what I am convinced to be the situation in this case.
I would like to go to the background for the GST and to address it briefly. I know that the opposition in particular tire of hearing about deficits and debt. The current financial strategy of the government is intended to direct our nation toward the elimination of deficit in due course and ultimately to the beginning of the repayment of our national debt.
Over the past five years, through the programs of the hon. Minister of Finance, we have been working our way slowly toward a reduction in the deficit and with the budget program and the strategy that was placed before us earlier this year, we are pointing in the direction of a balanced budget in the years of the early 1990s, and perhaps before the year 2000, to even a surplus where we can commence to pay down that debt and to start to reduce the burden on future generations.
There is only one way to stop that debt from growing larger. That is to reduce the deficit and work toward a balanced budget and eventually to achieve a surplus. I think we must give credit where it is due. The financial strategy that Michael Wilson introduced in 1984 has produced some positive results. Since September 1984
October 12, 1989

the total number of new jobs in Canada amounted to
I,	535,000. The unemployment rate has dropped from
II.	2 per cent in 1984 to 7.3 per cent in September, 1989. That is a dramatic accomplishment, a drop of close to 40 per cent in that period.
Canada's competitive position has gone from eleventh place in the world economic forum in 1983 to fourth in 1988. I think that the strategy that we have embarked upon does hold promise for Canada, a promise that will make us financially strong and responsible by the turn of the century, 10 years from now.
Unless we as citizens do accept the importance of our national responsibility, unless we are either willing to pay for the excellent standards of living we enjoy or to bear the restraint in reductions in the present levels of services, or a combination of both, then I am deeply convinced that the consequences of undisciplined continuity of deficits and debt will eventually lead us to the economic tragedy of hyperinflation, of currency devaluation, and a severe erosion in the future quality of life for coming generations in this country. The signs of that can be seen in countries like Bolivia, Argentina, Mexico and post-war Germany.
I believe it is paramount to understand that the goods and services tax is a critical and major component of the government's financial strategy for the 1990s. It is considered to be a most reliable and fair source of government revenue, essential to supplement the income tax program which itself was beneficially reformed in the past two years.
The goods and services tax is a value-added tax on consumption which will grow with the economic activity of our country. It has well become the most favoured consumption tax in the world and is now being used in some 48 countries, including 19 of the 24 members of the OECD, generally all among the world's most successful economies.
The motion today does not indicate whether it would terminate the existing federal sales tax, but we must recognize that this new tax replaces an existing federal sales tax that is hidden, that is regressive, that impacts on our competitive effectiveness for international export. It
Supply
is really a failed tax, the elimination of which is long overdue. Because it occurs on many capital costs and operating expenses which are not possible to isolate in our export pricing it, makes us less competitive in international markets and it indirectly favours imports to the disadvantage of our domestic producers.
By comparison, the new goods and services tax will be applicable broadly at the consumption level to all Canadians and on a very wide range of commodities, with relatively few important exceptions. Instead of different rates which are currently applicable to the FST, ranging from 9 per cent to 13.5 per cent, the new tax will have a standard rate of 9 per cent.
Based on the economic assumptions in the April budget, and in terms of comparable values in 1991 dollars, the existing federal sales tax collects tax revenues of $18.5 billion. The new goods and services tax will collect revenues of $24 billion. The difference at the beginning of $5.5 billion will be applied directly to fund special provisions of the GST program. This is the significant aspect of the GST program. It is an integrated tax reform system. It touches on increases in the income tax credit program, and of the $5.5 billion in new revenues, $2.4 billion will go to 9.3 million Canadian families who will benefit from increased tax credits at the lower income levels.
Another $700 million will provide for income tax reductions of 1 per cent in the middle tax range. Lastly, about $2 billion of that $5.5 billion will be required to cover the index benefits of indexation which the 2.5 per cent or 2.25 per cent inflationary impact of GST will bring about for those at the lower level of the income tax range for family allowance benefits and for old age pensions.
Finally, of the total of $24 billion, $200 million, or less than 1 per cent, will be required for administration of the new program. I believe that this tax program does shift the burden from those least able to pay to those most able to pay. The discretionary income of Canadians as is reflected in consumer purchases will support the tax, and the food exemption ensures that low income families will not be paying a disproportionate ratio of their income which is directed to basic groceries in the form of the new tax.

Supply
That alone is another measure that shifts the burden from those least able to pay to those most able to pay. The income tax credit does the same thing. The reduction by 1 per cent achieves a similar purpose. I should add that the unemployment insurance changes as embodied in Bill C-21 with the shift of premiums to employers and employed in high growth areas of Canada with the benefits payable to those who are unemployed in the lower growth areas of Canada also have the effect of shifting the tax burden to those best able to pay. This is a principle that this motion by the opposition calls for. I believe that that is already being accomplished.
I would like to wind up by saying that I believe the new goods and services tax program is not only a critical element in our nation's long-term financial strategy but a distinct improvement over the regressive federal sales tax which it is eliminating. Perhaps most important of all, because the GST does integrate effectively with the income tax program through the provisions of refundable tax credits and because it tends to balance the fairness of the total tax program more effectively away from those least able to pay, it is an instrument of financial fairness as well as of financial responsibility.
I believe that this motion is redundant and that its purposes are very significantly addressed in the government's current program.

speakerposition: Minister of Employment and Immigration; Minister responsible for the Status of Women
subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S. O. 81-PROPOSED GOODS AND SERVICES TAX
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. Immediately following these proceedings six Canadian women will be honoured in the other place for their outstanding contribution to women's equality in Canada. The occasion is the presentation of the Persons Awards celebrating Alberta's famous five. This is the sixtieth anniversary of the Persons case and therefore a very special occasion indeed.
I would like to invite all members to attend the reception immediately following that ceremony in Room 200, West Block, shortly after 7 p.m. I can promise them that status of women throw the best parties.

subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S. O. 81-PROPOSED GOODS AND SERVICES TAX
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would just like to join with the minister responsible for the status of women in commending her invitation to all members of the House and hoping that, as persons themselves, they will join in the celebration.

subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S. O. 81-PROPOSED GOODS AND SERVICES TAX
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S. O. 81-PROPOSED GOODS AND SERVICES TAX
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, we too join in celebrating 60 years of personhood for women. We would urge that all members join us in that celebration later this afternoon.
